lessons.title: Find spaCR on GitHub, PyPI and conda-forge
lessons.description: Find the official package and installer sources, compare the release available on each channel, and choose the matching installation tutorial.
objectives: Find the official download pages.
Choose the installation route for your computer.
Open the matching installation tutorial.
lessons.prerequisite: Open a web browser and decide whether you want a desktop installer or a Python environment.

scenes.narration: Choose how you want to install spaCR. Use a desktop installer for a ready-to-launch application, pip for a Python virtual environment, or conda-forge for a Conda environment. Start from the official spaCR links shown here.

On PyPI, find spaCR and read the installation command beside the current release. Copy that command when you are ready to install into your Python environment. The pip tutorial shows how to create and activate that environment first.
Use Project links to open the documentation, source repository or issue tracker. Bookmark the documentation so you can return to the module walkthroughs while working in spaCR.
On GitHub, open the spaCR repository. Main contains the release source, and nightly contains the latest development work. For a packaged desktop installation, open Releases and choose a release.

Expand Assets and download the installer for Windows, macOS or Linux. Keep the checksum file from the same release if you want to verify the download. The Platform installers lesson walks through launching the installer and opening spaCR.
On conda-forge, open the spaCR package page and check the available version. Package channels can update at different times, so select the version available through the route you choose.
The conda-forge command installs spaCR into your active Conda environment. Follow the Conda lesson to create that environment, install the package and launch the application.
Continue with pip, Conda or Platform installers. Once spaCR opens, move to the Home lesson, then the pipeline overviews to choose a workflow for your data.

objectives: Creare e attivare un ambiente Conda dedicato.

lessons.description: Apri un modulo da Home, trova gli strumenti collegati e i dati di esempio, poi scegli una pipeline da seguire.

lessons.title: Python API and batch commands
lessons.description: Find an analysis function, load saved settings, check the inputs and run spaCR from a terminal.
objectives: Find the installed batch commands and their Python functions.
Inspect a function signature and its API reference.
Check saved settings before running an analysis.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR and activate its Python environment. Follow the Regression tutorial to prepare paired score/count tables and save the analysis settings. Use your own file paths in the commands.

scenes.narration: Activate the Python environment where you installed spaCR. Import spacr and print its version with the command shown. Keep the version with your analysis notes so you can reproduce the same run later.

Run spacr-run with dash dash list to find the available batch commands. The list shows each command key and its Python function. Choose the command for your task, such as mask, measure or regression. Use the desktop application for interactive tasks such as labelling images in Annotate.

Run spacr-run with dash dash describe followed by regression. Read the required inputs, defaults and function name. Here, the batch command calls perform_regression in spacr.ml. Open that function in the API reference to read its parameters and returned results.

In Python, import the function you need and inspect its signature. This example imports build_report from spacr.report. Look up the same name in the API reference, prepare the required arguments, and call the function from your script or notebook.

Save the settings from your module workflow, then pass the file with dash dash settings. Add dash dash dry-run to check the configuration and input paths. In this Regression example, the settings pair phenotype scores with guide counts for each plate. Read the messages and correct any missing inputs before continuing.

To execute the analysis, run the same command without dash dash dry-run. Follow the console until the command finishes, then inspect the outputs described by that module’s tutorial and API page. Keep the settings file, input tables, package version and console log with the results.

lessons.title: Classify: learn from measured features
lessons.description: Load measurements, define classes, train a tabular classifier and inspect object scores and plate summaries.
objectives: Select the tabular family and a measured project.
Define classes and choose feature channels, model size and held-out wells.
Find model outputs, object predictions and summary figures.
lessons.prerequisite: Use Load test data in Classify and choose Load, then confirm the downloaded plate folder with Choose source data. For your own project, run Measure first. The example uses columnID values c1 and c2 as two classes; use labels appropriate to your experiment when working with your own data.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify and choose Tabular Machine Learning. This family uses the object measurements saved by Measure. It produces a fitted model and a score for each object with the required measurements.
Click Load test data and choose Load. Wait for the measured example to download. For your own data, select the project folder created by Measure, including its measurements database.

Use Choose source data to confirm the downloaded plate folder. Select the folder containing measurements. This gives the classifier access to the object tables and the metadata used to define classes.

Choose metadata as the class basis and define two Classes using column I D values c1 and c2. These labels distinguish the two plate columns in the example. To train from your own cell annotations, choose the annotation basis and the label column you created in Annotate.

Set Channel of interest to one for the example. This controls which channel-specific measurement features enter the model. For your own experiment, select the channel that contains the signal relevant to your classes.

Choose Random Forest, sixteen estimators and two worker jobs. Estimators controls the number of trees. More trees increase fitting work. Leave feature pruning and cross-validation off for this first pass; you can compare those choices after you have a working baseline.

Set Test size to one tenth and keep grouping by well. spaCR holds out complete wells, so the final fraction of objects can differ from the requested fraction. Read the resolved split in the console and make sure it suits your experiment.

Enable Plot, clear the search and press Run. The console shows feature filtering, the training and test split, model fitting and the saved output paths. Wait for the run to finish before comparing its scores.

Find the results under results, random_forest, channel underscore one. The database stores the predicted class in predictions and the class-one probability in ml_pred. Objects missing required measurements can remain unscored; inspect missing values when exporting a summary.

Browse the feature-importance figures and plate heatmap. With Predictions and mean grouping, a well value is the average of its binary predicted classes. Use the saved object scores for detailed review, and compare held-out performance before applying the classifier to another experiment.

lessons.title: Map Barcodes: from sequencing reads to counts
lessons.description: Load paired reads and library references, find barcode positions, apply the settings and save guide counts.
objectives: Download a small paired-read example and select matching reference tables.
Inspect barcode positions and orientation before applying a proposal.
Run mapping and inspect count and quality-control outputs.
lessons.prerequisite: Choose Load test data in Map Barcodes. The example uses SRR33531217 reads, the matching primers_3 column and row tables, and guide references. Use reference tables matching your own library when processing other reads.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Map Barcodes. The inputs are sequencing reads and reference tables that name the barcodes in your library. The output counts each observed combination, ready for sequencing quality control and downstream analysis.
Click Load test data and select both mates of the first archive run. Limit each file to ten thousand reads for this example, then wait for the paired sample to download.

Select the matching column, row and guide reference tables. Each table pairs barcode names with sequences. Keep those names consistent with the plate layout and guide identifiers used by the rest of your analysis.
Open Find barcodes and start the search. The preview samples both mates and checks barcode positions and orientations. Wait for the results before changing the main form.

Compare Observed with By chance, then inspect the proposed orientation, offset and verdict for each barcode. Prefer positions supported by many reads and distinct expected references. Open the verdict explanation if the result is uncertain.

Inspect the guide results for both mates. In this example, read one supports the reverse-complemented guide sequence and read two supports the stored orientation. Use the results for your library and read pair when choosing an orientation.

Check the row barcode as well. Here, read one supports its reverse complement and read two supports the stored sequence. Review column, guide and row together so the complete combination identifies the intended well and guide.

Open the read viewer to inspect individual reads. Use the colour legend to find the column, guide, row and anchor segments. Check that the proposed positions agree with the expected library structure.

Review the proposed extraction settings, then click Apply these settings to copy them into the form. The example uses an extraction window of eighty-nine bases. Check the updated fields before starting the run.

Follow the orientation notes when selecting your final reference files. For this example, select reverse-complemented copies of the row and guide references and keep the column reference as stored. Preserve every barcode name when preparing those copies.

Choose the downloaded read pair, two workers and chunks of one thousand reads. Enable annotated-read saving if you want to inspect individual assignments. Click Run; this mapping workflow uses the CPU.

When mapping finishes, inspect unique_combinations.csv and the quality-control outputs. The count table links column, row and guide names with read counts. Review unmatched and ambiguous assignments in Barcode QC, then pair these counts with phenotype scores in Regression.

lessons.title: Regression: from paired tables to results
lessons.description: Pair phenotype scores with guide counts, choose an inference method, run the example and explore guide and gene results.
objectives: Load paired score/count tables and choose an output folder.
Set the inference method, reporting level and analysis unit.
Run the example and inspect results with the accompanying diagnostics.
lessons.prerequisite: Open Regression and choose Load test data to obtain four paired score/count tables. Use a new output folder. A measurement database is optional for this score-and-count analysis; object-level views require the corresponding measured data and images.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Regression. This module relates phenotype scores to guide abundance. Start with a score table and a count table for each plate, then choose how to test and report associations.
In Input Tables, click Load test data and wait for the example to load. It provides four score tables and four count tables, paired by plate.
Inspect each paired row and check the plate name, score file and count file. Leave the optional measurement-database column empty for this example. Choose a new output folder for the analysis.

Switch to All settings and use the search box to find Inference. Choose nonparametric for this guide-permutation example. Use a parametric method when your question and design call for fitting predictors together.
Level chooses which results to report. Select both to obtain guide-level and gene-level results. Keep these testing families separate when reviewing adjusted significance.

Choose well as the analysis unit for this example. Review the response column, transformations, controls and excluded wells. Adapt these settings to the design of your own screen before running new data.
Minimum guide support controls how many wells must contain a guide before it is tested. Set it to two to follow this small example. Choose an appropriate support requirement for your experiment.

Set one hundred and ninety-nine permutations for a quick first run. More permutations give finer empirical p-value resolution and take longer. Choose a larger count when your final analysis requires it.

Set the permutation seed to zero to repeat the same randomization. Keep the example’s plate blocks and row and column nuisance terms. For your own data, choose blocks that respect which observations can be exchanged under the experimental design.
Choose none for Annotation source to run the example without gene-annotation lookup. For another screen, select annotations that match its organism and identifier system.

Clear the search, check the paired inputs and output folder, then click Run. Follow the console as the module aligns the tables, filters guides and calculates the results. Diagnostic figures are generated with the analysis.

When the run finishes, open Runs and select the saved analysis. Confirm the folder and settings before comparing it with another run. Rerun the analysis after changing settings if you want new results.

Open Results and use Level to switch between guide and gene results. Inspect the result table and interactive views. The saved results_grna.csv and results_gene.csv files contain the corresponding tables for further analysis.

Open the p-values view and the Diagnostics tool. Review the result distribution together with the permutation resolution, testing family and design warnings. Resolve important diagnostic concerns before interpreting associations.

Use the toolbar to open Volcano Explorer, Hit List or Investigate Hit for the next step. Their tutorials show how to inspect selected results. Keep the input tables, saved settings, result files and diagnostic reports together when sharing the analysis.

lessons.title: Make Masks: modificare le etichette e preparare immagini di addestramento
lessons.description: Apri coppie immagine-maschera, esamina e modifica gli oggetti, salva le misure e crea ritagli appaiati per l’addestramento.
objectives: Aprire immagini con le relative maschere di istanza ed esaminare gli oggetti con la lente.
Misurare campi appaiati e salvare un database di caratteristiche degli oggetti.
Correggere le etichette con Undo, disegno, divisione e filtri di dimensione.
Salvare le maschere revisionate e creare ritagli immagine-maschera per l’addestramento.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepara una cartella di immagini bidimensionali con i TIFF di etichette di istanza corrispondenti in una sottocartella masks. Ogni maschera usa il nome base del file immagine. Lavora su una copia quando ti eserciti con modifiche e ritagli. L’esempio usa immagini di ER e maschere cellulari dal progetto di microscopia scaricabile di Measure.

scenes.narration: Da Home, apri Make Masks in Tools. Scegli questo editor per esaminare e correggere le maschere di singole immagini. Apri la cartella di immagini ed etichette appaiate prima di scegliere uno strumento di modifica.
scenes.speech_text: Da Home, apri Make Masks in Tools. Scegli questo editor per esaminare e correggere le maschere di singole immagini. Apri la cartella di immagini ed etichette appaiate prima di scegliere uno strumento di modifica.

scenes.narration: Seleziona la cartella delle immagini. Per questo esempio, usa le immagini di intensità dell’ER e le maschere cellulari corrispondenti del campione di Measure. Mantieni uguali le dimensioni di immagine e maschera, e appaiati i nomi dei file.
scenes.speech_text: Seleziona la cartella delle immagini. Per questo esempio, usa le immagini di intensità dell’ER e le maschere cellulari corrispondenti del campione di Measure. Mantieni uguali le dimensioni di immagine e maschera, e appaiati i nomi dei file.

scenes.narration: L’editor carica l’immagine e la maschera corrispondente dalla sottocartella masks. Le etichette colorate identificano i singoli oggetti. Verifica che i contorni seguano i bordi nell’immagine. Se manca una maschera associata, parti da una maschera vuota e disegna gli oggetti che ti servono.

scenes.narration: Apri Magnifier settings. Seleziona Otsu e Region under the mouse per vedere in anteprima gli oggetti ottenuti per soglia intorno al puntatore. Scegli una modalità basata su un modello quando la soglia non separa bene i tuoi oggetti.

scenes.narration: Attiva Magnifier e passa sopra un oggetto per ingrandirne l’anteprima. Spostati su diversi oggetti per esaminare i contorni proposti. Fai clic per aggiungere gli oggetti delineati quando sembrano corretti, oppure disattiva Magnifier per continuare a modificare.

scenes.narration: Fai clic su Features per misurare coppie immagine-maschera. Aggiungi una riga per ogni campo e scegli le immagini di intensità e le maschere di oggetti corrispondenti. Controlla le assegnazioni manuali se l’abbinamento automatico dei nomi lascia file non assegnati.

scenes.narration: In ogni riga, seleziona l’immagine di intensità dell’ER in Channel 1 e l’immagine di etichette corrispondente in Cell mask. Ripeti per il secondo campo. Usa le immagini di intensità originali per misurare la fluorescenza.

scenes.narration: Controlla entrambe le righe, poi scegli le impostazioni di misura. Questo esempio usa un solo processo, una dimensione minima della cellula di un pixel e nessun ritaglio PNG salvato. Aumenta la soglia di dimensione per escludere gli oggetti piccoli quando è adatto al tuo esperimento. Fai clic su Measure.

Aumenta la soglia di dimensione per escludere gli oggetti piccoli quando è adatto al tuo esperimento. Fai clic su Measure.

scenes.narration: Al termine della misura, apri la cartella di output. La cartella measurements contiene measurements.db con le caratteristiche degli oggetti di entrambi i campi. Conserva il database con le immagini, le maschere e le impostazioni di origine, poi chiudi Features per tornare alla modifica.
scenes.speech_text: Al termine della misura, apri la cartella di output. La cartella measurements contiene measurements punto di bi con le caratteristiche degli oggetti di entrambi i campi. Conserva il database con le immagini, le maschere e le impostazioni di origine, poi chiudi Features per tornare alla modifica.

scenes.narration: Scegli lo strumento adatto alla correzione. Brush aggiunge pixel, Erase rimuove pixel ed Erase object rimuove un’intera etichetta. Draw aggiunge un oggetto delineato; Divide ne divide uno. Zoom ti aiuta a esaminare i bordi prima di apportare modifiche.

scenes.narration: Scegli Erase object e fai clic dentro l’oggetto da rimuovere. Controlla il contorno aggiornato e il numero di oggetti. Usalo per un’etichetta indesiderata, come detriti o un oggetto fuori dai tuoi criteri di analisi.

scenes.narration: Fai clic su Undo per annullare l’eliminazione. Redo la applica di nuovo. Usa questi comandi della cronologia per confrontare una modifica con la maschera precedente, poi torna alla versione che vuoi tenere.

scenes.narration: Seleziona Draw e traccia un contorno chiuso intorno a un oggetto mancante. L’editor lo riempie con una nuova etichetta. In questo esercizio il contorno è sullo sfondo, quindi annullalo prima di salvare. Per i dati di addestramento, traccia il bordo reale dell’oggetto.

scenes.narration: Usa Divide quando due oggetti a contatto condividono un’etichetta. Traccia un taglio attraverso tutta la regione unita ed esamina le etichette separate. Annulla la divisione se taglia un unico oggetto o lascia un bordo errato.

scenes.narration: Regola Display percentiles per rendere più facili da esaminare le strutture deboli. Questi controlli cambiano la visualizzazione e conservano i valori di intensità grezzi e le etichette. Torna a una visualizzazione uniforme quando confronti i campi.

scenes.narration: Imposta le aree minima e massima degli oggetti, poi premi Filter per rimuovere le etichette fuori da quei limiti. Scegli limiti adatti ai tuoi oggetti ed esamina cosa è stato rimosso. Il filtro modifica la maschera, quindi usa Undo se la soglia elimina oggetti utili.

scenes.narration: Dopo aver rivisto le modifiche, fai clic su Save mask. Se serve, riporta a zero i limiti di dimensione per disattivarli prima di passare a un altro campo. Conserva le immagini di origine e tieni il registro di revisione salvato insieme alle maschere modificate.

scenes.narration: L’intestazione contiene il resto degli strumenti per le maschere. Quando scegli i pesi, Model Zoo li trova e Model Compare mette due serie di maschere una accanto all’altra. Quando altri esempi vanno corretti, Curate e Open in napari ti riportano alla modifica.

scenes.narration: L’intestazione apre anche Model Compare, Model Zoo, Curate e Open in napari. Usa Model Compare per esaminare maschere una accanto all’altra, Model Zoo per scegliere i pesi e gli strumenti di revisione per rivedere o modificare altri esempi.

lessons.title: Image UMAP: explore measurements with image crops
lessons.description: Select measurement tables, build a UMAP embedding and click points to inspect the corresponding objects.
objectives: Load a measured project and choose its feature tables.
Control neighbourhood size, point spacing and the sampled row count.
Run the embedding, inspect crops and find saved results.
lessons.prerequisite: Follow Annotate and choose Load test data, then Load, to obtain the measured example and its image crops. Keep the downloaded plate folder. For your own data, complete Measure with saved crops before opening Image UMAP.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Image UMAP. Use it to explore similarities between measured objects while viewing their image crops. Start with a project containing a measurements database and the crops saved by Measure.

Under Source, choose Add project folders and select the example plate folder downloaded through Annotate. Review the available databases, rows and shared columns. You can add more project folders when you want to compare several datasets.

Choose the tables whose features you want to compare. For this example, select cell, cytoplasm, nucleus and pathogen measurements. Leave Resnet features off to use the existing measurements. Review missing-data and correlated-feature settings before running.
Set Row limit to four hundred for a quick first view and use two workers. Row limit controls how many objects enter the embedding. Increase it when you are ready to explore more of the dataset.

Choose UMAP as the reduction method. Each point will represent an object using two plotted coordinates. You can explore PCA through its linked tool when you want a linear projection and feature loadings.

Set Neighbours to fifteen and Minimum distance to zero point one. Neighbours controls the size of the neighbourhood used to build the map. Minimum distance controls how closely points can pack in the displayed embedding.
Set Random seed to forty-two so repeated runs with the same inputs and settings are easier to compare. Save your chosen feature tables and preprocessing settings alongside the seed.
Clustering assigns labels to groups after the embedding is built. This example uses DBSCAN with noise removal off. Inspect the crops within any group before using its label in a later analysis.
Enable Plot images and Plot points. Use twelve small crop images so the overview remains readable. You can inspect individual objects more closely in the interactive view after fitting.
Press Run and watch the console for feature preparation and embedding progress. Wait for the completed result. If you change the input tables or reduction settings, run again to produce a new map.

Inspect the embedding in Figures and open the results folder reported in the console. Keep the saved figure, selected measurement rows, metadata and cluster labels together so you can trace an interesting group back to its objects.
Enable Interactive to explore the fitted map. Zoom into a region and click its points. The view uses the completed embedding, so you can inspect different objects without fitting it again.

Click a point to show its crop in the side panel. Use the displayed object path to connect the image to its source record. Compare morphology across nearby points and across distant regions of the map.

Click another point to compare its crop. The sidebar also provides selection labelling and cluster-label propagation. Those controls save annotations, so choose the intended label and selection before applying them.

Open Image Scatter from the Image UMAP header to compare selected features directly, or open PCA for a linear projection. Continue with the linked tutorials for their input settings and saved outputs.

lessons.title: Activation Maps: inspect an image classifier’s saliency maps
lessons.description: Select a trained classifier and matching image crops, compare channel and image saliency, and open the saved maps.
objectives: Match the crop archive, model and preprocessing settings.
Run channel saliency with an image overlay.
Compare image saliency and locate the saved grids.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a trained image-classification checkpoint and a TAR archive of compatible image crops. Retain the crop-format marker when present and follow the model card’s channel order, image size and normalization. The example uses four RGB crops from Annotate and a ResNet18 model from Classify. Train or obtain a model whose preprocessing is known before starting.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify, then Activation Maps. This tool shows where a trained image classifier’s prediction is sensitive to the input pixels. Start with the model and an archive of crops prepared in the same way as its training data.

Select the crop archive in Dataset. This example contains four RGB cell crops from Annotate. Include the crop-format marker when packaging the images, and keep their filenames so you can connect each map to its original object.
Select the trained model and choose its model type. Here the model is ResNet eighteen. Read its model card and set Image size to one hundred and twenty-eight to match the training input.
Set Channels to the order expected by the model. In this example the selector uses one, two and three for the RGB input. Preserve that order when comparing maps from different images.
Set Normalize input to match training. The separate display normalization controls how the image appears in the saved overlay. Keep both settings consistent when comparing runs.
Choose saliency channel and enable Overlay, Plot and Save. This produces separate channel maps over the images. For the four-crop example, use a batch size of four and one worker, then click Run.
Follow the console until processing finishes. If the Figures panel is empty, open the output folder and inspect the saved batch grids. Check error messages and the saved results before continuing.

Open batch_0_grid.png from the method’s batch_grids folder. Match each occupied slot with its source crop; unused slots may be blank. The corner labels are model predictions. Compare salient regions with the original image and known object boundaries.
To compare a combined map, select saliency image and turn Overlay off. Run the same images again with the same preprocessing. Keep the two methods’ outputs in their respective folders.

Open the second saved grid. Image saliency combines the channel sensitivities into one map for each crop. Compare the highlighted regions with the channel maps. The displayed colours indicate the map scale; interpreting them requires checking the model and image context.

Leave Correlation off for this first walkthrough. Review examples from different classes, including prediction errors, before interpreting patterns. Use Classifier Evaluation to assess performance on independently held-out data.

Keep the input archive, model and model card, settings, maps and output database together. Return to the original crops to investigate unexpected regions, or compare another method using the same inputs.

objectives: Caricare le immagini e le maschere di esempio in Track preview.

lessons.title: Motility assay
lessons.description: Measure movement from tracked objects, inspect track filters, and save per-frame and per-well results.
objectives: Load a project containing tracked merged arrays.
Choose mask planes, track filters and acquisition units.
Run the analysis and find the movement tables and plots.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete a Timelapse run, or download and extract SYNTHETIC_motility_tracks.zip. Select the folder containing merged. The example has eight frames, nucleus intensity in channel 0, cell intensity in channel 1, tracked cell masks in plane 2 and nucleus masks in plane 3. It has no pathogen mask or physical calibration.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Measure, then use Time to open Motility Assay. Start with tracked images from Timelapse, or download the example archive below to follow along.
Extract the example and set Source to the folder containing merged. Choose cells as the tracked objects, nucleus channel zero and cell channel one. Leave the pathogen channel unset for this example.

Turn on Live to open Motility preview and choose the same project folder. Use the preview to inspect tracks and try filters before running the full analysis. Keep Propagate settings off while exploring temporary choices.

Set two intensity channels, tracked mask plane two, and pathogen mask plane minus one, meaning none. Preview all eight frames. In the preview, set both calibration values to zero for this uncalibrated example, then click Run preview.

At minimum track length three, the example has sixteen usable tracks. Review the trajectories, length distribution and speed summary. Speed is about one point four pixels per frame because the example has no acquisition scale or interval.
Min track length sets how many frames an object must span to enter the summary. Increase it to exclude brief tracks, and watch the retained count. Keep it at three for this eight-frame example.

Drop over-straight tracks excludes tracks above the chosen straightness threshold. Straightness is net displacement divided by total path length. Compare the retained tracks and plots before choosing a threshold; leave this filter off when straight movement is part of your experiment.

For acquired data, enter pixels per micrometre and seconds per frame from your microscope and acquisition metadata. With both values, the preview can express speed in micrometres per minute. To try the conversion on this teaching example, two pixels per micrometre and sixty seconds per frame change the mean to about zero point seven. Those are example values, not measured calibration.

Set the full analysis form’s pixel scale and frame interval as well; preview edits are separate until you propagate them. Check the chosen object, channels and filters before starting the run. Keep the acquisition values with your results.

Leave Reuse existing measurements off for the first run and enable the quality-control graphs. With no pathogen channel, leave infection quality control disabled. Click Run and follow progress in the console.

When the run finishes, open measurements, then measurements.db in the project folder. The selected table contains per-frame observations; its well_motility companion summarizes movement by well. Inspect the saved plots and their units before comparing conditions or exporting figures.

lessons.title: Train Cellpose: coppie verificate e procedura esplicita tramite API
lessons.description: Trova Train nel Cellpose Workbench, riconosci il difetto di importazione della sorgente e segui un vero addestramento Python di due epoche su sei coppie scaricabili immagine/maschera cellulare.
objectives: Trovare Train e Apply dentro Make Masks, non come tessere Home separate.
Verificare nomi abbinati e distinguere etichette esistenti da riferimenti revisionati.
Riconoscere l’importazione parziale e separare API e GUI difettosa.
Esaminare input, riscaldamento, pesi modificati e percorso verificato.
Distinguere perdita, valori di test segnaposto e lettura dei pesi dall’accuratezza indipendente.
lessons.prerequisite: Usa sei coppie, script registrato e manifesto collegati. I ritagli conservano intensità cellulare canale 1 e maschera cellulare piano 4 da campi reali; piano 6 significa patogeno. Etichette e oggetti tagliati NON sono riferimenti revisionati indipendentemente. Train perde ancora src e mantiene model_name=new_model pur importando i numeri; nessun training GUI parte. La chiamata spacr.submodules.train_cellpose usa destinazione nuova, due epoche, minibatch 1, learning_rate=1e-5, weight_decay=1e-5, target_size=512, senza aumento extra spaCR. normalize=False disattiva i percentili spaCR, non la divisione per il massimo né la normalizzazione Cellpose. Cellpose ruota/ridimensiona e usa patch interne di 256. Seed 19 iniziale, casualità interna conservata. CUDA al 65% su RTX 3090 e guardia RAM 100 GiB adatta soltanto a questa macchina. Verificati 3,145,728 valori e dodici pannelli; tutte le sei coppie restano nel training. Tassi 0 e 1.1111111111111112e-6; 345 di 347 tensori addestrabili modificati. Perdita salita da 1.496740683913231 a 1.5215517828861873. Nessun test, quindi gli zeri sono segnaposto. Checkpoint sotto models/cellpose_model/models letto con weights_only=True; il riepilogo omette il secondo models. Leggere non significa inferenza o accuratezza. Figura reale in visualizzatore esterno, mai inserita nella GUI. Originali, tentativi falliti e blocco GUI conservati. Nessuna richiesta AI, risposta, approvazione scientifica o pubblicazione.

scenes.narration: La prima epoca di riscaldamento ha tasso zero. La seconda usa un piccolo tasso positivo e consente aggiornamenti reali. Confrontando il checkpoint con i pesi iniziali, sono cambiati trecentoquarantacinque tensori addestrabili su trecentoquarantasette. Cambiare soltanto il diametro non supererebbe la verifica. Pesi diversi non dimostrano comunque un buon modello.

lessons.title: Apply Cellpose: segment a folder and inspect masks
lessons.description: Choose a segmentation model, process the supplied images and inspect saved masks and live size filters.
objectives: Select images, model weights and segmentation settings.
Run Apply and locate the saved mask TIFFs.
Inspect live results and compare object-size filters.
lessons.prerequisite: Extract the linked Apply Cellpose example into a new folder. It contains three single-channel cell images and a settings reference. Select its images folder as Source. This walkthrough uses the stock cpsam model; for a custom model, choose compatible weights and settings for your images.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Make Masks, then its Cellpose Workbench. Choose Apply to segment images with an existing model. Use Train when you want to learn new weights from curated image-mask pairs.

Extract the linked example and set Source to its images folder. It contains three single-channel cell images, each five hundred and twelve pixels square. If you use the recorded settings file as a reference, replace its source path with your extracted folder.

Select cpsam and leave Custom model empty for this example. Set Channels to zero, normalization percentiles to two and ninety-nine, Diameter to thirty, Flow threshold to zero point four and Cell probability to zero. Adjust these settings after inspecting a few representative fields from your own experiment.
Enable Save and Verbose, choose a batch size of one, and click Run in Apply. Follow the console as each image is processed. Review failures before proceeding to measurement.

Open the masks subfolder inside Source. Each image has a same-stem mask TIFF. Inspect the figures beside the original images, paying attention to missed objects and joined cells. The flow panel shows model directions used for segmentation.

Turn on Live preview and choose an image with the image picker. Open Live settings and check the channel and normalization controls. Collapse Console and System to give the preview more room if needed.

Compare the preview with the saved batch mask. Preview and Apply use different processing paths in this example, so they can produce different boundaries and counts. Review the saved TIFFs when deciding whether the batch outputs are suitable for measurement.
Use the mouse wheel to enlarge an area on both preview canvases. Inspect touching objects and dim boundaries, then zoom back out to check the complete field.

Open Live settings and increase Minimum cell area to remove small objects from the preview. The cutoff is in pixels; choose it according to your object sizes. Close the dialog to inspect the filtered result.

Compare the filtered outlines with the original image. Changing this live filter updates the preview without rewriting masks already saved by Apply. Rerun the batch with the intended settings when you need new saved outputs.

Return Minimum cell area to zero to restore the unfiltered preview. Keep the input images, model identity, settings and saved masks together. Use Make Masks for corrections or Measure to extract object features from the reviewed masks.

lessons.title: Model Compare: compare saved segmentation masks
lessons.description: Load two masks of the same image, run the downloadable comparison helper and inspect overlap scores and overlays.
objectives: Choose masks of the same field with matching pixel geometry.
Run the saved-mask comparison example.
Read the agreement table and inspect boundary differences.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and extract the linked Model Compare example. It provides one image, two saved masks and a Python helper. Use an environment with spaCR installed and choose a new output folder outside the extracted inputs. The example compares two preprocessing choices with the same cpsam weights; assessing accuracy requires reviewed reference labels.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Make Masks and choose Model Compare. Use this workflow to inspect segmentation differences on the same image. This walkthrough uses the linked saved-mask example and its Python helper.

Keep the model weights and preprocessing settings with each set of masks. When preparing your own comparison, use the same fields and pixel geometry so object overlaps refer to corresponding image locations.

Extract the linked example. The inputs are image.tif, batch.tif and preview.npy. Both masks describe the same field; they were produced with the same model and different preprocessing settings. Keep their original filenames for the supplied helper.

Run the supplied helper in your spaCR Python environment. Set source to the example input folder and output to a new results folder. The printed summary lists object counts, matched objects, mean matched overlap and adjusted Rand index. Higher agreement means the masks are more similar; it does not by itself establish which mask is correct.

Open comparison.png. Compare the two mask overlays with the image and inspect splits, merges and boundary shifts. The right panel highlights pixels where foreground membership differs. Check touching-object boundaries in the overlays as well.

Open comparison.csv for the numerical results and retain it with comparison.png, the inputs and the recorded settings. Use reviewed reference masks and representative fields when comparing segmentation accuracy or choosing a model for your experiment.

lessons.title: Model Zoo: choose a model and try it on your images
lessons.description: Open Model Zoo, find or download a checkpoint, inspect its details, and choose a small image set for a trial.
objectives: Open Model Zoo and scan a local model folder.
Choose a model family and version, then inspect its details.
Run a small image trial and inspect the resulting masks and quality summaries.
lessons.prerequisite: Extract the linked example and use its images folder for the three-field trial. Choose an installed Cellpose segmentation model, or download a suitable checkpoint through Model Zoo. For your own trial, prepare a few representative TIFF, PNG, NPY or NPZ images.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Make Masks, then choose Model Zoo. Use this page to find a segmentation model and try it on a small image set.
Click Choose folder and select your model directory to scan it. If you type the path instead, click Scan. Turn on the source headings you want to browse, such as Cellpose or local models.

Select a model family and use its Version control to choose the checkpoint. Read the details for its image type, training information and local path. For a remote checkpoint, choose a Save to folder and click Download before trying it.

Extract the linked example and choose its images folder under Test on fields. Set the field count to three. For your own images, start with a small set that includes typical fields and difficult cases.
Select the local segmentation model and click Test on fields. Wait for the trial to finish. Larger images and models can take longer, especially on a CPU.

Select a result row to inspect its mask preview. Check boundaries, touching objects and missed objects against the image. Use the object count and quality flags to help find fields that need closer inspection.

Review the field summaries, then keep the chosen checkpoint path for your analysis module. To compare two different model families on the same images, select both rows and choose Compare the two selected. Use the version control to try another version of one family.

lessons.title: Annotator Agreement: compare independent annotation passes
lessons.description: Choose annotation columns, compare agreement and inspect the crops where labels differ.
objectives: Open the example database and select two annotation passes.
Read pairwise agreement and the confusion matrix.
Inspect disagreements and compare three annotation passes.
lessons.prerequisite: Extract the linked Annotator Agreement example and keep its database with the crop images. It contains sixteen images from the Annotate example and three artificial teaching-label columns, DEMO_A, DEMO_B and DEMO_C. For your own analysis, use independently collected annotations of the same images.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Annotate, then choose Annotator Agreement. Use this tool to compare labels collected in separate annotation passes. The results help you find images that need review.

Open the example database. Keep the extracted crop folders beside it so the image previews can load. The DEMO columns contain artificial teaching labels; use your own independent annotation columns when assessing agreement in a study.
Select at least two annotation columns from the list. For this example, start with DEMO A and DEMO B. Check the column names so you compare the intended passes.

Click Compute agreement. The two selected passes share twelve labelled crops. Three more crops have a label in only one pass, and one has neither label. Pairwise agreement uses the crops labelled by both passes.

Read the pairwise results. The passes agree on nine of twelve crops, giving seventy-five percent agreement and a Cohen kappa of zero point five. Read these values alongside the number of shared labels; a small sample gives an uncertain estimate.

Open the confusion matrix. Rows represent DEMO A and columns represent DEMO B. The diagonal contains matching labels: five for class one and four for class two. The off-diagonal cells contain the three disagreements.
Select a disagreement to view its crop and the labels assigned by each pass. Compare the image with your class definitions. To revise a label after review, return to Annotate.

Add DEMO C and click Compute agreement again. The pairwise table now shows all three pairs. Each pair uses its shared labels, while the overall summary uses crops labelled in all three selected passes.

Read the overall Fleiss kappa and the unanimous agreement summary. This example gives a Fleiss kappa of about zero point six six three. Review the disagreement list as well: it can include a crop that has labels in only two of the three passes.

To focus on one pair again, select only A and B and click Compute agreement. The results stay in this comparison view; your annotation columns remain in the source database. Continue in Annotate to collect another independent pass or review the identified disagreements.

lessons.title: Plaque Assay: count plaques and measure their areas
lessons.description: Open the synthetic example, choose saved masks or model segmentation, inspect a preview, and read the per-image and per-plaque results.
objectives: Open Plaque Assay from Toxoplasma and select the image folder.
Choose a model, inspect a preview and set area filters.
Run the analysis and inspect counts, areas and calibration in the output database.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and extract SYNTHETIC_plaque_example.zip. It contains four grayscale TIFF images and their saved label masks. Use a working copy when trying new segmentation. Have a local plaque checkpoint available or download one through Model Zoo. The synthetic example has no physical calibration.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Toxoplasma, then choose Plaque Assay. Start with a folder of plaque images. This walkthrough uses the linked synthetic example so you can practise selecting masks, adjusting the preview and opening the results.
Download and extract the example. Set Source to SYNTHETIC_plaque, the folder containing the TIFF images and the masks subfolder. Keep a working copy if you plan to generate replacement masks.

Leave Masks off to analyse the supplied label masks. Switch Masks on when you want the selected model to segment the images first. For new segmentation, choose a plaque model and review its diameter and detection thresholds on a representative image.

Leave well detection off for this example. For images containing a whole plate, use well detection to separate the wells. If you know the image scale, enter pixels per micrometer; a known physical well diameter can also provide calibration. Record formation time in hours when it is known. Leave unknown calibration values unset.

Set Plaque model to a local checkpoint. If you need one, open Model Zoo and download a plaque model, then enter its local path. The analysis resolves this model setting even when it reuses saved masks.
Open Live preview and Live settings. Check the selected model and image before running the preview. Match the model in the preview to the one you plan to use for the full analysis.

In Model Zoo, select the plaque model, choose a Save to folder and click Download. Wait until the model is available locally, then select that checkpoint for the preview. Keep its saved path for later runs.

Choose an example image and click Run preview. Switch View between outlines and coloured masks to check whether the predicted regions follow plaque boundaries. Inspect several representative images before running a plate.

Raise Min area to hide small predicted regions. Watch which objects disappear, and adjust the threshold to the smallest plaque you intend to measure. Change one setting at a time so its effect is clear.

Lower Min area to bring smaller regions back; zero removes this lower area cutoff. Check the final preview and the batch settings before Run. A preview shows the selected image; Run produces the analysis outputs.

Press Run and follow the console until the analysis finishes. With Masks off, the example reads the supplied labels and writes masks/plaques_analysis.db. The database contains the counts and areas for the images in Source.
Open Help, then Database browser. Select plaques_analysis.db in the masks folder. Leave Edit mode off while inspecting the output, and choose a table from the table list.
Open summary for an overview by image. Match rows using their filenames. The supplied synthetic masks contain four, three, two and one objects. Average size reports their mean area in pixels.

Open stats to compare each image’s plaque count, mean area and area spread. The standard deviation describes the range of plaque sizes within that image. Use independent experimental replicates when comparing biological conditions.

Open details to inspect individual plaque areas. Physical-area columns are empty when calibration is unavailable. Save the database together with the images, masks and settings. Experimental growth estimates additionally require a known scale to estimate time, or a known time to estimate scale; validate the reference curve for your assay.

lessons.title: Recruitment: measure marker enrichment around parasites
lessons.description: Choose a measured project, map the marker channel and conditions, set object filters, then inspect recruitment ratios by host cell and well.
objectives: Select a project containing linked cell, nucleus, pathogen and cytoplasm measurements.
Set the marker channel, plate conditions and object filters.
Run Recruitment and read the host-cell and well CSV results.
lessons.prerequisite: Start with a project from Measure containing measurements/measurements.db and linked cell, nucleus, pathogen and cytoplasm tables. Include merged images to display image overlays. The example uses an ER marker on channel 1; use the channel mapping and condition labels recorded for your own project.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Toxoplasma, then choose Recruitment. Use this analysis to compare marker intensity in parasite-associated regions with the surrounding host-cell cytoplasm. Begin with a project whose objects and intensity channels have already been measured.
Set Source to the project folder containing measurements/measurements.db. Keep the cell, nucleus, pathogen and cytoplasm tables together. Include the merged image folder if you want image overlays.

Set Channel of interest to the marker you want to measure. Channels use zero-based numbering: one means the second image plane. This example uses channel one for the ER marker. Choose the channel that matches your acquisition.

Set Channel dims to the channels needed for the auxiliary recruitment summaries. For a first run, use the same single channel as Channel of interest so the main ratio and additional intensity summaries are easy to compare.

Check the cell, nucleus and pathogen channel mapping against the measured project. The example uses cell one, nucleus zero and pathogen three. Keep the mapping with your settings so overlays and filters refer to the intended signals.

Enter the cell, pathogen and treatment labels, then map each label to its plate rows or columns. Only annotated wells enter the analysis. Match these assignments to your plate layout, including the positive and negative controls.

Use the size ranges to exclude objects outside the areas you intend to analyse. Areas are in pixels, and the bounds are strict. Pathogen area is aggregated within each host cell for this analysis, so choose its range for the cell-level total.

Set Nuclei limit and Pathogen limit to control which host cells are retained. A nuclei limit of one keeps single-nucleus cells. Raise a limit to include cells with more associated objects, then inspect how many cells remain.

Start with broad intensity ranges so you can inspect the initial results. Narrow a range when you have a defined intensity-based selection rule. Target intensity minimum applies an additional cutoff to the marker’s cell intensity.

Check the channel used by each intensity filter before narrowing its bounds. With the example’s mapping, the nucleus intensity filter uses channel three and the pathogen intensity filter uses channel one. Keep the broad example ranges while learning the workflow.

Set Cells per well to the minimum source-cell count required for a well to remain in the analysis. This setting filters wells, while the object filters select cells. Inspect the final retained counts as well as the threshold.

Enable Plot to display available image overlays and use Plot number to limit how many are shown. Keep Plot control enabled if you want the control-intensity figures. Use the plots to check channel choices and filtering before interpreting the ratios.

Press Run. Follow the console as the module joins the measurements, applies conditions and filters, calculates ratios and writes the results. Wait until the analysis finishes before opening the output tables.

Inspect the recruitment plot. The main value divides the host cell’s aggregated pathogen mean intensity by its cytoplasm mean intensity on the selected marker channel. Values above one indicate enrichment relative to that reference. Read the numeric exports for ratios below the plotted range or invalid denominators.

Inspect the well summary and compare the control conditions. Each well averages its retained cell ratios; condition plots summarize those well values. Error bars show between-well standard deviation. The cell table represents host cells with aggregated pathogen measurements.

Open results/cells.csv for retained host-cell measurements and results/wells.csv for well summaries. Keep both files with the saved settings. Check cell counts, condition labels and finite ratios before comparing experiments, and use independent wells as the experimental replicates.

lessons.title: Invasion Assay: valutare la colorazione esterna e totale
lessons.description: Assegna due canali di colorazione, scegli il riferimento di colorazione, esegui l’analisi ed esamina le classificazioni di invasione e la sensibilità alla soglia.
objectives: Scegliere il database delle misure e assegnare le colorazioni esterna e totale.
Impostare i pozzetti di riferimento e i controlli della soglia, poi eseguire l’analisi.
Esaminare distribuzioni, denominatori per pozzetto e tabelle dei risultati salvate.
lessons.prerequisite: Estrai l’esempio sintetico di Invasion Assay collegato e usa il suo riferimento delle impostazioni. Il database contiene 1.800 misure sintetiche di parassiti; i nomi delle condizioni e i risultati sono illustrativi. Per il tuo saggio, usa un protocollo di colorazione a due colori validato, con colorazione esterna prima della permeabilizzazione e colorazione totale dopo, ed esamina immagini rappresentative.

scenes.narration: Da Home, apri Toxoplasma e scegli Invasion Assay. Parti da un database di misure che contenga le intensità dei parassiti per le colorazioni esterna e totale. Usa il campione sintetico collegato per esercitarti ad assegnare i canali, scegliere la soglia ed esaminare i risultati.
scenes.speech_text: Da Home, apri Toxoplasma e scegli Invasion Assay. Parti da un database di misure che contenga le intensità dei parassiti per le colorazioni esterna e totale. Usa il campione sintetico collegato per esercitarti ad assegnare i canali, scegliere la soglia ed esaminare i risultati.

scenes.narration: Estrai il campione e imposta Source sulla sua cartella invasion, che contiene measurements/measurements.db. Inserisci il riferimento delle impostazioni allegato e sostituisci il segnaposto di Source. Il campione contiene pozzetti di riferimento e due condizioni del saggio.
scenes.speech_text: Estrai il campione e imposta Source sulla sua cartella invasion, che contiene measurements/measurements punto di bi. Inserisci il riferimento delle impostazioni allegato e sostituisci il segnaposto di Source. Il campione contiene pozzetti di riferimento e due condizioni del saggio.

scenes.narration: Imposta Outside channel su uno e Total channel su zero. La colorazione esterna si applica prima della permeabilizzazione; quella totale, dopo. I parassiti positivi alla colorazione esterna sono classificati come attaccati, quelli pari o inferiori alla soglia esterna come invasi. Controlla l’ordine dei canali di acquisizione quando usi le tue misure.

scenes.narration: Seleziona mean in Intensity statistic per corrispondere alle colonne del database di esempio. Per il tuo saggio, scegli una statistica disponibile adatta alla colorazione ed esamina oggetti rappresentativi. Lascia Minimum total intensity a cento per questo campione.
scenes.speech_text: Seleziona mean in Intensity statistic per corrispondere alle colonne del database di esempio. Per il tuo saggio, scegli una statistica disponibile adatta alla colorazione ed esamina oggetti rappresentativi. Lascia Minimum total intensity a cento per questo campione.

scenes.narration: Imposta Stain baseline wells sulla colonna uno, usando c1. Queste misure a colorazione negativa stabiliscono la soglia e sono escluse dai denominatori del saggio. In Pathogen plate metadata, assegna vehicle alla colonna due e inhibitor alla colonna tre.

scenes.narration: Imposta Control quantile a zero virgola novantanove e lascia vuoto l’Outside threshold fisso. Le misure di riferimento determinano allora la soglia, circa ventidue virgola otto in questo esempio. Controlla la soglia applicata nell’output prima di interpretare le classificazioni.

scenes.narration: Imposta Threshold sensitivity a zero virgola venticinque. Vengono così valutate anche soglie del venticinque per cento sotto e sopra quella scelta. Confronta l’intervallo di efficienza di invasione ottenuto per vedere quanto il risultato dipende dalla scelta della soglia.

scenes.narration: Imposta Extracellular class su classify per il campione. Per gli oggetti senza collegamento a una cellula ospite, classify usa la colorazione, attached li assegna agli attaccati ed exclude li rimuove dalla popolazione valutata. Scegli questa impostazione tenendo conto della qualità delle assegnazioni alle cellule ospiti.

In un esperimento, confronta queste distribuzioni con immagini colorate rappresentative e indaga le colorazioni esterne deboli.

lessons.title: Replication Assay: contare i parassiti per vacuolo
lessons.description: Carica le misure dei parassiti, scegli l’identità del vacuolo, esegui l’analisi ed esamina le distribuzioni dei conteggi e le esportazioni.
objectives: Scegliere un database di misure e il relativo identificatore di vacuolo.
Impostare i filtri di assegnazione alla cellula ospite e di dimensione, poi eseguire l’analisi.
Leggere le distribuzioni per pozzetto e trovare le tabelle dei risultati salvate.
lessons.prerequisite: Estrai l’esempio sintetico di Replication Assay collegato. Contiene un database di misure e un riferimento delle impostazioni, con 1.992 righe di parassiti in 480 vacuoli distribuiti su dodici pozzetti. I nomi delle condizioni e le misure sono dati didattici. Per il tuo saggio, usa parassiti misurati con assegnazioni ai vacuoli verificate e repliche sperimentali indipendenti.

lessons.title: Training Runs: confrontare curve e impostazioni
lessons.description: Carica i log di addestramento, sovrapponi le metriche, confronta le impostazioni ed esplora le fold della validazione incrociata.
objectives: Trovare le esecuzioni salvate e selezionare quelle da confrontare.
Sovrapporre metriche di addestramento e validazione ed esaminare le differenze di impostazioni.
Passare dalle singole fold alla loro media e deviazione standard.
lessons.prerequisite: Scarica ed estrai l’esempio sintetico di Training Runs collegato. Le sue curve sono dati di esercitazione. Per la tua analisi, seleziona una cartella principale che contenga i file train.csv e validation.csv salvati insieme alle impostazioni di ogni esecuzione. Conserva risultati di valutazione indipendenti con il modello quando ne valuti le prestazioni.

scenes.narration: Da Home, apri Classify, poi Training Runs. Usa questo strumento per confrontare i log di avanzamento e le impostazioni di addestramenti salvati. Il campione collegato contiene curve sintetiche per esercitarti con i comandi.

scenes.narration: Procedi nella schermata in ordine: scegli una cartella per trovare le esecuzioni, selezionale nell’elenco, poi scegli Metric e Folds e fai clic su Overlay selected. Parti dalla cartella principale che contiene le tue esecuzioni.

scenes.narration: Estrai il campione collegato e fai clic su Choose folder. Seleziona la sua cartella training_runs, poi conferma la scelta. Per i tuoi progetti, seleziona una cartella principale che contenga le cartelle delle esecuzioni e i relativi log CSV salvati.
scenes.speech_text: Estrai il campione collegato e fai clic su Choose folder. Seleziona la sua cartella training_runs, poi conferma la scelta. Per i tuoi progetti, seleziona una cartella principale che contenga le cartelle delle esecuzioni e i relativi log CSV salvati.

scenes.narration: Analizza la cartella ed esamina le esecuzioni trovate. Il campione contiene gli esempi baseline, tuned e cross_validated, più una voce incompleta. Seleziona le esecuzioni utilizzabili che vuoi confrontare.

scenes.narration: Fai clic su Overlay selected. Le curve di addestramento sono tratteggiate e quelle di validazione continue. Leggi ogni esecuzione e ogni suddivisione nella legenda. Ogni curva termina alla propria ultima epoca registrata.

scenes.narration: Esamina il confronto delle impostazioni sotto il grafico. Evidenzia differenze come dimensione del batch, numero di epoche e tasso di apprendimento. Usalo per capire cosa è cambiato tra le esecuzioni prima di interpretarne le curve.

lessons.title: Report: create a document from project results
lessons.description: Choose a completed project, select the output format and figure limit, then generate and read its report.
objectives: Choose a completed project and inspect its available report sections.
Set the format, figure limit and output filename.
Generate the report and inspect its results, settings and provenance.
lessons.prerequisite: Start with a completed spaCR project containing its saved settings, measurements and figures. You can reuse the project from the External Masks tutorial. Report collects files already present in the project.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Report. Use this tool to collect a completed project’s results, figures and settings into a document.
Click Choose run folder and select your project. For this example, use the two-field project from External Masks, keeping its measurements, settings and figures together.
Read the processing status after the scan. Complete means the recorded processing steps finished. Review the available quality-control results separately when assessing the analysis.
Check the section list to see which project artifacts are available. A missing section remains labelled in the report. Add the relevant analysis outputs to the project if you need that section.
Choose HTML, PDF or Both under Format. HTML opens in a browser; PDF provides a document version. This example uses HTML.
Set Embed at most to limit the number of raster figures included in the document. Vector PDFs are listed as source files rather than embedded previews. Use a smaller limit for a compact report.
Click Choose output and enter the destination filename. Check that the selected format and extension agree. Before sharing the report, review any project paths and metadata it includes.
Press Generate report and wait for the written-file confirmation. Open the saved HTML file in a browser to inspect the result.
Use the contents links to jump between sections. Start with the processing summary, then review figures, result tables and saved settings.
Open Key figures to find the project’s figures. Follow the listed file locations for vector PDFs, or inspect embedded raster previews when available.

Review Statistics and result tables for the available object tables and their row counts. This cell-only example has matching cell and cytoplasm regions, so treat them as measurements of the same cells.
Expand Saved settings to inspect the configuration retained with the project. Keep the report together with the project files when sharing an analysis that refers to external figures.

lessons.title: Plate Queue: run several prepared projects
lessons.description: Add the current project or drop prepared folders into a queue, run jobs in order, and continue after a controlled stop.
objectives: Add prepared projects with their saved module settings.
Run the queue and stop between jobs.
Find each project’s results and clear completed queue entries.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare a project and its saved module settings. For practice, use two copies of the Recruitment example in separate folders; they contain the same data and are not biological replicates.

scenes.narration: Prepare the first project in its analysis module. In Recruitment, choose Import settings and open the project’s settings CSV. The example uses two separate copies of the same measured data to practise running several jobs.
Check Source, the channel mapping and the condition labels. Save the settings you want the queue to use, then leave this project open.
Open Help, then Plate queue. The queue runs one item at a time in the listed order.
Choose Add current plate. A new row stores the current module and settings. Check its module, source and label before starting the queue.

Drag another prepared project folder onto the queue. Its saved settings identify the module, and the dropped folder becomes its source. Use separate project folders when each job needs separate output files.
Choose Run queue. The first row changes to running while later items remain queued. Watch the status and elapsed time to follow progress.
Press Stop when you want the queue to finish its current item and pause before the next one. Wait until the active job finishes.
The completed row now says success and the next row remains queued. Choose Run queue again to continue with the remaining item.

When both jobs finish, open each project’s output folder. For Recruitment, inspect the cells and wells CSV results. Use Recruitment directly when you want its figure workflow; this queue does not display or save those plots.
Choose Clear finished to remove completed entries from the list. Their project folders and saved results remain available.

lessons.title: External Masks: measure images with supplied object labels
lessons.description: Assign image and mask files, preview their pairing, then create a measured spaCR project with object tables and crops.
objectives: Assign intensity images and label masks to the correct roles.
Choose channels, output location and measurement options.
Preview the pairing, run Measure and inspect the output project.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare matching intensity images and integer-labelled masks with the same spatial dimensions. Each object needs its own positive integer label; zero is background. The example reuses two image and cell-mask pairs from the Import Project tutorial.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Import Project, then choose External Masks. Use this tool when you already have segmentation labels and want spaCR to measure the corresponding images.

Prepare matching intensity images and labelled masks. This example uses two image and cell-mask pairs. Keep each pair aligned and use filenames or metadata that let the importer match the correct field.

Click Add folder for the image folder and again for the masks. Review Use as: choose Image for intensity files and Mask for labels. Set Mask type to the compartment represented by each mask, such as Cell.
Set Use as to Ignore for any group you want to leave out. Its files stay on disk. Keep the image group and the masks required for your analysis included.
Restore Image for the example’s intensity group. Check the Image and Cell-mask assignments before choosing the destination.

Set Dst to a new project folder. Choose Layout, Z handling and Plate naming to match your files. This example uses flat layout, the first Z plane and index-based plate naming. Use acquisition metadata when original well identities must be retained.
Choose the intensity Channels to measure. This example’s TIFFs each contain one intensity plane, so select channel zero and leave Normalize off. Channel numbers refer to the files you are importing.
Choose whether to measure cytoplasm. With cell masks alone, the derived region covers the whole cell. Supply the interior compartment masks when you need them excluded from that region.

Under Object Crops, enable Save PNG and choose cell in Crop mode. Set PNG size to two hundred and twenty-four by two hundred and twenty-four. Select channel zero for this single-channel example’s PNG mapping.
Choose the measurement features you need, then enable Save measurements. Use N jobs to set concurrency. Start with a small input set while learning the settings and inspecting the resulting crops.
Enable Preview only and press Run. Check the proposed image-to-mask pairings, field count and channel layout in the plan. Correct any assignment before writing the project.
Turn off Preview only and press Run again. The tool prepares the project’s images and masks, then runs Measure to calculate object features and create the requested crops.
Inspect the intensity image beside the supplied labels. Check object boundaries, missing objects and image-to-mask alignment before interpreting the measurements.
Browse the object montage to inspect the extracted crops. Use the figure viewer to move between fields and check that the selected channels and crop size show the objects clearly.

Open measurements/measurements.db for the object tables and data for annotation crops. Keep conversion_map.csv and the source manifest with the project so imported fields remain traceable. Continue in Annotate to label the crops, or use the measurement tables in a downstream analysis.

lessons.title: Align & Stitch: plan and write an image mosaic
lessons.description: Choose image tiles, set their acquisition layout, inspect the registration plan, and write the mosaic with its coordinates.
objectives: Choose tiles and set the grid, overlap and registration channel.
Inspect the planned positions and registration quality.
Write the mosaic and retain its coordinate database.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and unzip the nine-tile example below, or prepare image tiles with known acquisition order, overlap and a useful registration channel. The example uses overlapping crops from one microscopy field to provide a practice layout.

scenes.narration: From Home’s Tools category, open Align and Stitch. Choose the tiles, review their layout with Plan, then use Write stack to create the mosaic.

Download and unzip the example below, then select its tiles folder. It contains nine overlapping crops arranged in a three-by-three grid. For your own acquisition, keep the original tile order and stage metadata available.

Set the grid to three by three, row-major order and overlap zero point two five for this example. Match these settings to your acquisition; use serpentine order when alternate rows were acquired in opposite directions.

Set Reference channel to the image plane used for registration. This example uses channel one, the second plane with zero-based numbering. Choose a channel with visible structure across overlaps; the resulting placement applies to all image channels.

Set Minimum confidence for accepting a registration and Neighbour radius for the nearby tiles to compare. The example uses zero point three and one, with feather blending across overlaps. The band-buffer budget controls memory used by the image writer.

Press Plan. Inspect the registered, nominal and unplaced tile counts and the proposed canvas size. The layout shows tile positions. Review any nominal fallback or unplaced tiles before writing the mosaic.

Click a tile to inspect its coordinates, confidence, residual and contributing pairs. Use these details to investigate unexpected positions, then adjust the registration settings and plan again if needed.
Choose an output folder and a coordinate-database path. Leave Overwrite off when creating a new result. Once the plan and destination are ready, press Write stack.

Wait for the completion summary and open the output stack. Inspect the overlaps and object boundaries in the mosaic. Keep the coordinate database and source tiles with it so downstream locations can be traced back to the acquisition.

lessons.title: Plate Viewer: esaminare i pozzetti ed esportare una tabella di heatmap
lessons.description: Carica le misure di esempio, confronta caratteristiche e conteggi per pozzetto, esamina i singoli pozzetti ed esporta la tabella filtrata.
objectives: Aprire Plate Viewer da Graph Builder e caricare le misure di esempio.
Scegliere una caratteristica, un’aggregazione e un numero minimo di oggetti.
Esaminare i dettagli dei pozzetti ed esportare la griglia dei pozzetti corrente.
lessons.prerequisite: Usa Load test data in Plate Viewer per l’esempio scaricabile, oppure apri il file measurements.db del tuo progetto misurato. L’esempio contiene 2.341 cellule in quattro pozzetti; usa misure che coprano l’intera piastra quando valuti pattern spaziali.

scenes.narration: Da Home, apri Graph Builder in Data, poi scegli Plate Viewer. Usalo per riassumere le misure degli oggetti per pozzetto ed esaminarne la distribuzione sulla piastra.
scenes.speech_text: Da Home, apri Graph Builder in Data, poi scegli Plate Viewer. Usalo per riassumere le misure degli oggetti per pozzetto ed esaminarne la distribuzione sulla piastra.

scenes.narration: Fai clic su Load test data per aprire l’esempio scaricabile. Per i tuoi dati, scegli un database di misure o la sua cartella di esecuzione e fai clic su Open. L’esempio contiene quattro pozzetti misurati.
scenes.speech_text: Fai clic su Load test data per aprire l’esempio scaricabile. Per i tuoi dati, scegli un database di misure o la sua cartella di esecuzione e fai clic su Open. L’esempio contiene quattro pozzetti misurati.

lessons.title: Database Browser: filter and export measurements
lessons.description: Open a measurement database, select columns and rows, and export the result.
objectives: Open and browse a measurement table.
Select columns and filter rows.
Export the matching records.
lessons.prerequisite: Have a spaCR measurements.db file or a run folder containing one. Measure’s example project provides a database after measurement.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Database Browser to inspect and export measurement tables.
Choose measurements.db, or the run folder containing it, and open the database.
Select the table you need. Choose cell for cell measurements, or a different object table for that object’s features.
Read the total row and column counts, then inspect the displayed page. Use the page controls to move through larger tables.
Search column names to locate a feature. Select the columns you want to view and export.
Build a filter by choosing a column, an operator and a value. Apply it to select matching records across the full table.
Check the filtered row count and inspect the matching records. Adjust or clear the filter to change your selection.
Choose Export and a destination file. The export includes all matching rows and your selected columns, while keeping the source database unchanged.

lessons.title: Format Converter: anteprima e conversione di file immagine
lessons.description: Seleziona una cartella di origine, controlla i nomi di destinazione e le assegnazioni dei canali, poi converti le immagini e riprendi il lavoro già completato.
objectives: Scegliere le cartelle di origine e di destinazione con il layout di acquisizione corretto.
Visualizzare in anteprima nomi di destinazione, campi e assegnazioni dei canali.
Convertire i file e usare Resume per i campi già completati.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepara una cartella di file immagine supportati e conserva i loro metadati di acquisizione. Puoi esercitarti con le due immagini TIFF del tutorial Import Project. Imposta il layout e la gestione di Z in base alla tua acquisizione.

scenes.narration: Da Home, apri Import Project e scegli Format Converter. Usalo per preparare i file immagine e i nomi dei file per il passo successivo dell’analisi.
scenes.speech_text: Da Home, apri Import Project e scegli Format Converter. Usalo per preparare i file immagine e i nomi dei file per il passo successivo dell’analisi.

scenes.narration: Il convertitore lavora in una sola direzione: da Source, attraverso Preview, verso Destination. Preview mostra dove finirà ogni file di origine prima che venga scritto qualcosa, così puoi controllare le assegnazioni; poi Convert li scrive.

scenes.narration: Scegli la cartella che contiene le immagini di origine. Questo esempio usa due TIFF a canale singolo. Tieni a disposizione i metadati di acquisizione originali per controllare i nomi convertiti.

scenes.narration: Scegli una nuova cartella di destinazione. Il convertitore vi scrive le nuove immagini insieme a un file di corrispondenze; conserva a parte le immagini originali.

Per la cartella piatta dell’esempio, scegli l’opzione delle immagini direttamente nella cartella di origine e seleziona la regola di denominazione delle piastre che ti serve. Per un albero di cartelle per piastra e pozzetto, scegli il layout corrispondente.

lessons.title: Import Project: bring images, masks and measurements into spaCR
lessons.description: Choose matching images, instance masks and measurement tables, review their mapping, and create a spaCR project.
objectives: Match images, masks and measurement rows.
Review and save the column mapping.
Import the project and inspect its outputs.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare corresponding image files, instance-label masks and a measurement CSV. Keep each field’s original plate and well identity, and use documented measurement units.

scenes.narration: From Home’s Data category, open Import. Use this screen to bring existing images, instance masks and measurements into a spaCR project.

Pick the import tool by what you start with: Import Images or Format Converter for images alone, External Masks for images with masks. This screen takes images, masks and a measurement table together.
Choose the image folder. The example uses two microscopy fields with one intensity channel and matching cell labels. Keep a record of each file’s original plate, well and field.
Choose the Cell mask folder and press Add. Each object needs its own integer label. Add further mask classes when you have corresponding labels for the same fields.
Choose the measurement CSV. Match ImageNumber to each field and ObjectNumber to its mask label. Use both identifiers to distinguish objects across fields.
Enter micrometres per pixel when you know the calibration; otherwise leave it blank. Check that area and intensity columns retain their documented units.
Press Preview to inspect the proposed column mapping and joins before creating the project. Review the suggested foreign-prefixed names and their scientific meaning.
Select a target cell and press F two to edit its name. A reserved-name conflict disables Import when Refuse the import is selected; choose a distinct target name or use the Rename policy.
Read the join report and resolve unmatched rows or objects. In the example, all one hundred and three measurement rows match mask objects.
Give the imported area a clear name, such as foreign reviewed area pixels squared. Review the source, target, transform and units together.
Use Save mapping to keep the reviewed column definitions as a CSV. Keep the mapping with your images, masks, measurement table and acquisition identities.
