Use Load mapping to reuse saved definitions. Review the resulting plan whenever source columns, labels or units differ.
Press Import and read the completion report. The example writes two image files, two masks and two merged arrays, with one hundred and three rows in each of two object tables.
Open the project and inspect the imported measurements. The foreign columns table records their origin. Use Measure when you want spaCR to calculate new features from the images.

Keep the conversion map with the project and check its plate, well and field assignments. Generic file names may receive new coordinates, so resolve their original identities before plate-level analysis.
Continue in Database Browser to inspect the tables or in Annotate to review object crops. Retain the reviewed mapping with the completed project.

lessons.title: Batch Runner: configure and run a queue
lessons.description: Add module settings, arrange dependencies, run jobs, and inspect their separate logs.
objectives: Add jobs with their settings and dependencies.
Save, run and continue the queue.
Inspect each job’s log and outputs.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare the input data and exported settings JSON for each job. The example runs three image conversions into separate output folders.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Batch runner. Use it to queue module jobs with their settings files, execution order and separate logs.
Choose the module and click Choose settings. For this example, select convert and the JSON settings for the first microscopy field.
Check the source and destination in the settings, add a descriptive label, then click Add job. Use a separate output folder for each conversion.

For the second job, enter convert one in After to make it depend on the first. Add a setting override when this job needs a different value. Set any input paths explicitly; a dependency controls order.
Add further jobs and review their identifiers, labels and dependencies. Select a row to load its configuration into the editor.
Use the move controls to arrange jobs. A dependency must appear before the job that needs it; read any validation message and correct the order.
Click Validate after arranging the queue. Resolve the listed problems until Run queue becomes available.
Choose On failure to continue with independent jobs or stop at the first failure. Set Stop after to limit consecutive failures.
Click Save queue to store the plan as JSON. Use Load queue to reopen it later, keeping the referenced settings files and inputs available.
Click Run queue. To pause between jobs, press Stop; the current job finishes and the remaining jobs stay unrun.
Click Run queue again to continue with the remaining jobs. Watch each row’s status as the queue progresses.
Select a row to read its log and inspect errors or output paths. For the conversion example, check the reported field and channel identifiers.
Open each output folder and inspect the converted images and conversion record. Keep the queue JSON, settings and logs with the results.

lessons.title: Distributed Jobs: configure an execution target
lessons.description: Create an execution profile and prepare a module job for another workstation or cluster.
objectives: Create a profile for your execution target.
Configure paths and backend options.
Prepare submission and inspect job status.
lessons.prerequisite: Arrange access to a target with spaCR, its dependencies and your input data. Export the module settings you intend to run. Replace the illustrative host and paths shown here with your own.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Distributed jobs. Start by creating an execution profile for the workstation or cluster you want to use.
Install compatible spaCR dependencies on the target and make the input data available there. Set up SSH keys or your provider’s command-line authentication outside spaCR.
Choose New profile. Enter a descriptive name and select the backend. Complete the required fields shown by the form.
For SSH, enter your host, remote work directory and spaCR runner. Save the profile, then reopen it whenever you need to update these settings.
Set the local and remote dataset roots when the same data has different absolute paths on the two machines. This rewrites settings paths; arrange shared storage or copy the files separately.
For Slurm, choose the partition, time limit and accelerator request supported by your cluster. Keep the host and directory settings appropriate for its login environment.
For a cloud or custom command, enter submit, status and cancel argument templates, plus log retrieval if needed. Include the required settings and external-ID placeholders shown by the controls.
Save the changes you want to retain, or use Cancel to leave the profile unchanged. Poll interval sets how frequently to check job status.

Select the profile, module and its exported settings, then use Submit when the target is ready. Monitor status and logs in the job table. Use Cancel job to stop a selected job, and inspect its results at the configured output location.

lessons.title: Classifier Evaluation: inspect predictions and errors
lessons.description: Load a saved evaluation bundle, inspect leakage and confusion counts, and filter predictions for review.
objectives: Load a bundle and review leakage.
Inspect confusion counts and confidence groups.
Filter predictions and locate saved figures.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and unzip the linked saved-results example. It contains predictions, tables and figures; crops require your matching experiment in Annotate. The example shares wells between training and test data, so use it to learn the inspector rather than estimate independent-well accuracy.

scenes.narration: Open Classify, then Classifier Evaluation. Use this inspector to explore a saved evaluation bundle after producing predictions.
Download and unzip the example below. Click Browse and choose the folder containing evaluation manifest dot json.
Read Summary for the number of predictions and the recorded class names. The example contains two hundred thirty-four predictions across two classes.

Open Leakage audit before interpreting accuracy. This example flags wells shared between training and test data. For an independent-well evaluation, prepare a split with separate wells and rerun training and evaluation.
Open Confusion matrix. Rows are recorded classes and columns are predictions. The diagonal shows agreement; off-diagonal cells identify disagreements to review.
Click a disagreement cell to list its examples. The selected cell contains eleven disagreements, grouped by confidence.

Change Confidence threshold to choose which disagreements enter the high-confidence list. Raising it from zero point seven five to zero point nine five leaves two in the high list and nine in the low list.
Review the selected examples alongside their images and annotations. Use the displayed explanations as prompts for investigation, and check the evidence before changing labels.
Open Per-plate metrics to compare results by plate. This example has one plate; a multi-plate bundle provides separate rows for comparison.
Open Calibration to compare predicted probability with observed class frequency. Check each bin’s count when interpreting the differences.
Open Predictions and type a sample or well identifier to filter the records. In the example, r five underscore c two selects one well’s predictions.
Clear the filter to restore all records. To open crops in your own project, first load the matching experiment in Annotate; the downloadable results example contains no crops.
Find the saved calibration and confusion figures in the bundle folder. Check labels and readability before using them in a report.
Keep the leakage audit with reported metrics. Use Training Runs to compare saved training progress, and return to Annotate when image or label review is needed.

lessons.title: Run History: inspect past jobs and restore settings
lessons.description: Find saved runs, inspect settings and logs, and load a previous configuration into its module.
objectives: Find runs using filters and search.
Inspect saved settings, files and problems.
Restore settings for a new run.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete a spaCR job to create a local run record. The example browses records from conversion, Recruitment and Regression runs.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Run history to browse the run records saved on this computer.
Click Refresh to load available records. Select a run to inspect its details, and drag the divider if you need more room.
Choose a module and status, then enter a search term to narrow the list. For example, select convert and Success to find completed conversions.
Open Files and models for recorded input and output details. Runs that skipped file hashing can have an empty inventory; use the output paths in settings or logs to find their results.
Clear or adjust the filters if the table is empty. Search terms and status selections work together.
Select a Recruitment run and read Overview for its elapsed time and recorded file counts. These summarize that saved execution.
Open Settings to inspect its source folder, channels and object filters. Scroll through the saved configuration before deciding to reuse it.
Open Files and models to inspect recorded paths, sizes and hashes. Keep the referenced project files available when you need to revisit the analysis.
Open Environment for recorded software versions and seeds. Use Copy path to locate the run’s journal folder.
Open Warnings and failure to read warnings attached to a completed run. Investigate relevant warnings before using its results.
Choose Failed to find unsuccessful jobs. Read the traceback and software versions when diagnosing a problem or preparing a bug report.
Return to the desired run and choose Load settings in module. Review the restored controls and current input paths before pressing Run.
Keep the journals you need with your project records. Use Clear all only when you intend to delete run records. Open Report to create a project summary.

lessons.title: Classify: choose a model and explore its results
lessons.description: Choose image or feature classification, load example data, inspect prediction results and open the related tools inside Classify.
objectives: Choose Computer Vision for images or Tabular Machine Learning for measurements.
Start with test data and follow the matching training walkthrough.
Inspect predictions and open evaluation, feature and training tools.
lessons.prerequisite: Open Classify from Home. Use Load test data for an example project. For your own project, prepare object crops or measured features and class labels from annotations or experimental metadata.

scenes.narration: Open Classify from Home. Start by choosing the classifier family. The image and tabular lessons linked here each walk through a complete example.
Choose Computer Vision to learn from object images. Choose Tabular Machine Learning to learn from measured feature columns. Measure provides these inputs, and Annotate lets you add object labels.
For the tabular example, click Load test data and choose Load. Select your class labels and feature settings, then follow the tabular lesson to train the model and save predictions.

After the tabular run, inspect the prediction heatmap and saved object scores. Objects with missing required measurements may remain unscored. Check the evaluation results to decide whether to revise your labels, features or model settings.

For image classification, follow the Computer Vision lesson to prepare labelled crops, choose a model, and set the training, validation and test splits. After training, inspect the evaluation figures and saved predictions.
Open Classifier Evaluation from the top-right tools. Select a saved evaluation bundle to inspect predictions, metrics and the data split.

Open Explain CV to relate an image classifier’s predictions to measured features. Supply the image prediction results and the corresponding measurements, then inspect which features explain the scores.
Open Activation to view which image regions influence model responses. Select the trained checkpoint and use the same image channels and preprocessing as during training.
Open Training Runs to compare saved training histories. Select runs with compatible metrics and data splits, then inspect their learning curves and settings.
Open Feature Explorer to compare measured features between selected groups. Choose the groups and filters, then inspect the feature ranking and plots.

Keep your trained model, predictions and evaluation results in the run folder. You can use object scores in Regression together with matching guide counts. The linked module lessons show the next steps.

lessons.title: Curate: edit masks and tracks
lessons.description: Practise brush edits, track splitting and joining, and save the corrected files.
objectives: Edit a label mask with the brush and undo controls.
Split, join and save tracks.
Preserve source files and curation history.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the synthetic practice archive and work on copies. Keep separate backups of masks and their .curation.json sidecars before reopening: saving a reopened mask currently replaces its earlier edit log.

scenes.narration: Open Make Masks, then Curate to edit label masks and tracks. Download the synthetic practice example below and keep an untouched copy.
Browse to the example’s integer-label TIFF. Each object has its own label, with zero reserved for background. Use the TIFF example for this walkthrough.
Set Brush radius to eight and click New to select a new label. Click an empty part of the practice image to paint a small region.
Click Undo stroke to remove the last brush edit. Paint again and inspect the result before saving.
Click Save mask to write the working TIFF and its curation sidecar. Before reopening, preserve both files in a new backup folder; the download includes a checkpoint script for this step.
Keep each session’s backup and edit notes. Reopening a mask starts a new in-memory log, and another save replaces its sidecar with that session’s history.
Browse to the tracks CSV and select tracks to review. Join accepts tracks with non-overlapping frame ranges; an overlap produces a message to resolve first.
Select track two, set Split at frame to four, and click Split. The later frames move to a new track while the earlier frames retain the original identifier.
Select the two non-overlapping halves and click Join to combine them. Click Save tracks to write the CSV and its separate curation sidecar.
Use Delete only for tracks you intend to remove. To discard an unsaved change, reopen the last saved CSV.
Inspect the reopened tracks and saved history. Keep originals and reasons for edits, and rerun any downstream analysis affected by corrected masks or trajectories.

lessons.title: Illumination: estimate and inspect a correction model
lessons.description: Choose image channels, estimate an illumination field, inspect its QC figure, and reuse the saved model.
objectives: Select representative fields and intensity channels.
Estimate and inspect an illumination model.
Reuse the model in Mask or Measure.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a merged image folder with representative fields from each acquisition group. The example uses the sixteen fields from Measure’s downloaded plate example. Know which stored planes contain intensities and which contain labels.

scenes.narration: Open Measure, then Illumination to estimate a correction model for uneven image brightness.
Set Source to the merged folder containing image arrays. Use representative fields from your acquisition; the example uses sixteen fields from one plate.
Set Channels to the stored intensity planes you want to correct. The example uses channel zero. Check your channel mapping and exclude label-mask planes.
Enable Illumination correction before estimating a field. When it is off, Run completes without creating a correction model.

Choose an estimator and its settings. For the polynomial example, use degree four and leave Illumination model empty to estimate a new field. Inspect the result for structures that belong to cells rather than illumination.
Enable Illumination per plate to fit separate acquisition groups. Set Maximum fields to a representative sample; the example includes all sixteen available fields.
Set Illumination dark from your camera calibration when available. It is an additive offset in raw counts; zero is the example setting.
Enable Illumination QC and choose a missing-model policy. With error selected, a missing plate correction stops processing so you can resolve it.
Press Run and read the saved model path in the console. This step estimates the model; enable it in a subsequent analysis to apply the correction.
Open the saved illumination QC PNG in the illumination folder. Use an image viewer if it does not appear in the Figures panel.
Inspect the estimated illumination field for smooth brightness variation and unwanted cell-shaped structure. Correction subtracts the dark offset and divides by this mean-one field.
Compare the before and after radial profiles. Use additional fields to assess how well the correction works beyond the images used to fit it.

To reuse the model, set its path and enable correction in the intended Mask or Measure workflow. Keep its channels, plate identities and settings with it, and avoid correcting the same intensities twice.

lessons.title: Data Manager: inspect usage, clean up and archive
lessons.description: Review project storage, preview a cleanup plan, and move a project to an archive destination.
objectives: Inspect project disk usage.
Review and apply a cleanup plan.
Move and rescan an archived project.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a completed spaCR project and keep an independent backup before cleanup. The example uses a copy of the project produced by External Masks.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Data manager. Choose a completed project to inspect its storage and plan cleanup or archiving.
Click Choose project and select the project root. Read Usage for its files, disk space and registered artifacts.
Open Prune and select the artifact types to consider. Leave measurement databases and model weights unchecked when you want to keep them, then click Show what can be deleted.
Review the proposed files, space saving and recovery information. The example selects the object-crop folder. Keep the inputs and settings needed to regenerate anything you remove.
Click Delete to review the final file list. Deletion cannot be undone, so check the paths and your backup before acknowledging the plan.
Use Cancel if you want to keep the files or revise the selection. Acknowledging the list enables the final Delete action.
Confirm Delete when the plan is correct. Read the result for the number of removed files and space recovered.
Review the updated Usage scan. Removed artifacts may remain listed as missing with their recorded recipe; regenerate them through the appropriate module when needed.
Open Archive and choose an empty destination outside the source project. Click Show what would move and inspect both paths.
Click Move to review the confirmation. Archive moves the project, so keep any separate backup you need before proceeding.
Confirm Yes to move the project. Keep the manifest at the destination and the archive log left at the original location.
Select the destination as the project and scan it again. Check the moved files and update any external references that still point to the old location.
Use Database Browser to inspect measurement tables, Report to make a project summary, and Data Manager for storage maintenance. Keep the archive records with your project documentation.

lessons.title: Project Browser: find and inspect projects
lessons.description: Search project folders, inspect recorded stages, and identify the next tool to open.
objectives: Discover projects using roots and search depth.
Inspect artifacts and recorded stages.
Choose the next relevant tool.
lessons.prerequisite: Choose folders containing your spaCR projects. Completed External Masks and Format Converter examples can be used for practice.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Project browser to find project folders and inspect their recorded outputs.
Click Add folder and choose a search root. Depth zero checks that folder itself; increase the depth when projects are inside subfolders.
Set Depth to one and click Scan to include folders immediately below the root. Inspect the resulting project rows.
Read State and Stage alongside the files found on disk. A folder without an artifact registry may show unknown even when it contains converted images.
Add further search roots to include other projects. Select a row to inspect it; if details are blank after a rescan, select another row and return.
Drag the divider to widen the details. Review recorded artifacts, unregistered files and the source of the last-run timestamp.
Open Stages to see which expected outputs are present. Use What could run next to choose a relevant workflow, then check that module’s required inputs.
Click a column heading such as Size to sort projects. Click it again to reverse the order.
Adjust Depth and scan again when you need a narrower or wider search. A directly selected project remains discoverable at depth zero.
Select a root and click Remove to stop searching it. This removes the search location from the list while leaving its files on disk.
Open Run History for job records, Database Browser for measurements, or Data Manager for cleanup and archiving. Use the relevant module tutorial to continue the analysis.

lessons.title: Napari Bridge: edit and return a label mask
lessons.description: Open an image and mask in napari, edit labels, and save the corrected mask back to spaCR.
objectives: Open corresponding image and label files.
Edit and undo changes in napari.
Return and inspect the saved mask.
lessons.prerequisite: Install the optional napari dependency and unzip the synthetic example into a new folder. Keep an untouched backup: Take the mask back overwrites the selected working mask. Close and reopen the viewer between saved editing rounds.

scenes.narration: Open Make Masks, then Napari Bridge. Use it to edit an existing label mask with its intensity image as a reference. Keep an untouched backup of the mask.
Download and unzip the synthetic example. Choose mask dot tif for Mask and image dot tif for Image, then press Open in napari.
Select the mask Labels layer in napari. Label zero is background; each object label has a display colour. Make edits on the labels layer.
Return to spaCR and use Take the mask back to import the viewer’s current labels. If you have made no changes, the status reports that the mask is unchanged.
For practice, select label eighteen, choose Fill, and click the object labelled two. Inspect the changed label before importing it.
Use Undo to reverse the last viewer edit. Repeat the Fill operation when you are ready to keep the change.
Click Take the mask back in spaCR. Review the changed-pixel count, then inspect the saved mask and its correction-history sidecar.
Click Close viewer and reopen the mask before the next editing round. This makes the saved mask the starting point for subsequent corrections.
After the next edit, take the mask back and inspect the result again. Close the viewer when finished, keep the correction history, and rerun measurements affected by the changed labels.

lessons.title: Barcode QC: inspect read depth and choose a cutoff
lessons.description: Load mapped counts, review well and guide coverage, and compare abundance thresholds.
objectives: Choose count inputs and QC settings.
Inspect coverage and positional effects.
Compare thresholds and keep the resulting tables and plots.
lessons.prerequisite: Use plate_1_unique_combinations.csv from the downloaded example-screen data in the Regression tutorial, or your own mapped count table. Choose a new output folder. Supply mapping-QC and barcode-reference files when you need checks that depend on unmapped reads or the expected library.

scenes.narration: Open Map Barcodes, then Barcode QC. Start from a mapped count table; the linked Regression example provides one for practice.
Set Count data to your count table and choose a new output destination. The example contains mapped reads across three hundred eighty-four wells.
Set Target gRNAs per well from your experimental design and choose the summary method used to derive the cutoff. The example uses five and median.
Set Starved read fraction to flag wells with low reads relative to the plate median. The example uses zero point one. Review flagged wells before excluding them.
Enable Plot and Save, then press Run. Add mapping-QC or reference inputs when you want their corresponding checks; the count table alone describes observed mapped reads.
Read the completion log and saved output paths. Investigate errors against the selected inputs before using the results.
Open barcode QC dot PNG and threshold sweep dot PNG from the output folder. Use an image viewer if the Figures panel is empty.
Inspect read depth, row and column effects, and guide representation. Compare with a reference library when you need to identify expected guides that are missing entirely.
Inspect the threshold sweep. In this example, a cutoff near one point two one percent of each well’s reads gives a median of five guides while retaining about fifty-eight percent of mapped reads.

Compare retained reads, retained wells and wells above the guide target as the cutoff changes. Choose a cutoff appropriate to your design; the guide target does not establish single-guide attribution.
Keep the recommendation, sweep table, plots and settings with the source counts. Use the chosen cutoff consistently in the downstream analysis and record the reason for your choice.

lessons.title: Hit List: filter candidates and export a shortlist
lessons.description: Load Regression results, filter by q-value, guide count and agreement, then export the selected candidates.
objectives: Open the example Regression results with the supplied companion.
Filter candidates and read their effects and guide agreement.
Export the selected rows as CSV, Markdown or HTML.
lessons.prerequisite: Extract Hit_List_real_results_companion.zip and activate your spaCR environment. The current Regression Hits shortcut does not reveal the panel; run python hit_list_companion.py and Browse to the extracted results folder instead. The companion does not connect Investigate. Use results_gene.csv wells_with_gene for supporting well counts: exported n_obs=0 is not the actual support. The example contains no genes passing q <= 0.05.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Regression and choose Hits. If the panel stays hidden, use the companion script supplied with this lesson to open Hit List.
Extract the linked example and activate your spaCR environment. Run python hit_list_companion.py. In the companion window, click Browse and select the extracted results folder.

The example loads three hundred twenty-five genes. Widen columns to read effect, P, q and guide agreement. Effects are standardized marginal effects. For supporting well counts, read wells_with_gene in results_gene.csv; the exported observation-count zero is unavailable support.
Set Max q to zero point zero five. This example has no passing genes, so the table becomes empty. Restore Max q to one to browse all candidates.
Set Minimum guides to two. One hundred seventeen genes remain with at least two tested guide rows. This filter keeps the original q-values.

Set Minimum agreement to one. Fifty-seven candidates remain whose tested guides all share the gene effect sign. Read agreement alongside q: these candidates still do not pass the significance threshold.
Enable Hide controls to remove the control row from this view, leaving fifty-six candidates. Disable it again to include that row in the later export.

Clear the other filters, choose Direction up and set Minimum absolute effect to zero point one. Sixteen rows remain. Choose your thresholds for your analysis, then restore these controls before the next step.
Enter an identifier in Search to find its row. An unmatched query leaves the table empty. Clear Search to restore the current filtered population.

For export, set two guides, full agreement, controls included and an empty search. Export the fifty-seven selected rows as CSV, Markdown or HTML. CSV preserves numerical detail. Save the filter choices alongside your files.

Clear the filters to return to all three hundred twenty-five genes. Keep shortlist exports separate from the original results. For Python, use build_hit_list, then filter and the CSV, Markdown or HTML writers; check each format’s row limit.

lessons.title: Methods & Results: draft and export a run report
lessons.description: Select a completed run, build its report, review the recorded settings and results, and export Markdown.
objectives: Select the project, run journal and matching result folder.
Build a digest and review the Methods, Results and Caveats tabs.
Copy the report text or export Markdown with the run digest.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete the Regression example first. Keep its project folder, run journal and guide_permutation results together. Review inferred settings, analysis versions and statistical thresholds before using the generated text in a report.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Regression, then Methods and Results. Use this tool to draft a report from a completed analysis. This walkthrough continues with the saved run from the Regression example.

Choose the project folder, the run journal and the matching regression-results folder. Leave Classifier empty for this regression example. Confirm that all selected files belong to the run you want to describe.
Click Build digest, then read the Methods and Results tabs. Check the analysis version against the saved run environment; the exporter version can differ from the version that performed the analysis.

Read Caveats and compare seed entries by name with the saved settings. A permutation seed and a global seed refer to different generators. Leave an unrecorded historical seed unknown when editing the report.
Open Run digest to inspect the structured settings and source records. Compare them with the prose and review warnings about missing reports or inferred defaults before sharing the draft.

In Results, inspect effect sizes and corrected q-values together. This example has no genes below a q-value threshold of zero point zero five. Describe the listed rows as ranked candidates when editing a heading that calls them hits.
Click Copy sections to copy the displayed Methods and Results. Review the copied text against the source records. Use Export Markdown when you also need the structured run digest.
Click Export Markdown and choose a new filename. The file contains both report sections and the run digest as an appendix. Keep an original draft and save your reviewed revisions separately.

Draft with AI is optional and sends the digest to your configured provider. Review its contents before using that option, then check any generated text against the saved analysis. You can also use build_digest, render_methods and render_results from Python.

lessons.title: Run Compare: compare saved runs
lessons.description: Choose two saved runs, inspect settings and count differences, and check available result comparisons.
objectives: Select baseline and comparison runs.
Inspect settings and count differences.
Locate available result comparisons.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and unzip the linked snapshots. Follow its README to run prepare_run_compare_download.py in your spaCR environment with a new destination folder. For your own comparisons, preserve each run’s outputs before they are overwritten.

scenes.narration: From Home’s Data category, open Run Compare to inspect outputs recorded for two runs.
Download and unzip the snapshot example. Follow its README to run the preparation script with a new destination folder.
Click Browse and select the prepared comparison folder. Keep original projects and their run snapshots available for your own comparisons.
Choose a baseline run as A and the comparison run as B, then click Compare. Check their module names and recorded versions.
Enable Show unchanged settings to include matching values. Expand entries to inspect the configuration used by each run.
Open Counts to compare object totals. Delta is B minus A. The example has matching counts; inspect the relevant images and measurements when you need to understand a difference.
Open Hits when both runs have registered regression results. The example contains Measure snapshots, so no hit comparison is available.
Choose two distinct runs. If the same run is selected on both sides, use the warning to correct the selection.
Keep both output snapshots and the settings that explain their differences. Use Run History for individual logs and Regression for the underlying hit results.

lessons.title: Control Charts: monitor controls across plates
lessons.description: Load a campaign table, select controls and baseline limits, inspect alerts, and export the plotted points.
objectives: Choose the measurement and control population.
Set the baseline and alert rules.
Inspect alerts and export chart points.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the synthetic campaign CSV below, or prepare a well-level table with plate identity, run order, a measurement and control labels. The example illustrates thirty plates with programmed drift.

scenes.narration: Open QC, then Control Charts to monitor repeated controls across a campaign. The practice CSV uses synthetic plates and a programmed drift.
Download the example CSV below, click Load table and select it. It contains thirty plates, each with three wells for each control type and three sample wells.
Match Plate, Run order, Measurement and Control column to the table. Under Control is, select neg for the negative controls. An empty selection includes all rows.
Choose Sigma from to control the variation estimator. Auto uses the subgroup estimator here, because each plate contains three selected control wells.
Choose Rules for the alerts you want to inspect. The example uses Limits only to focus on points outside the three-sigma limits. Changing a setting redraws the chart.
Set Baseline plates to twenty. The first twenty plates establish limits for the series. Read the report and rule table to locate flagged later plates.
To inspect positive controls, clear neg and select pos. Review their means and limits separately, then return to neg to continue the example.
Adjust Baseline plates when your planned reference period differs. The tool requires at least eight plates; choose a stable baseline appropriate to the assay.
Click Export points and choose a CSV destination. It saves plate identities, means, subgroup sizes, limits, baseline membership and fired rules.
Keep the input CSV, selected controls and baseline settings with the exported points. Use the flagged plate identities to investigate acquisition or assay changes.

lessons.title: Pipeline Graph: inspect outputs and dependencies
lessons.description: Open a project’s artifact graph, inspect missing outputs, and copy its dependency diagram.
objectives: Open the artifact graph for a project.
Inspect paths, states and dependencies.
Copy the diagram and refresh its records.
lessons.prerequisite: Choose a spaCR project with registered outputs. The External Masks example supplies measurements and crops; the Data Manager lesson shows how a removed artifact appears.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Pipeline graph to inspect a project’s recorded outputs and dependencies.
Browse to the project folder. If the graph is empty, check whether that folder has registered artifacts; existing files can be present without registry records.
Choose the measured project to display its artifact boxes. The example includes measurements, crops and a resource log, with a removed crop folder marked missing.
Click an artifact and widen the details with the divider. Inspect its path, role, run identifier, production time and software version.
Select a Missing artifact to find its recorded path. Its displayed size describes the saved record, so check the actual location when investigating absent files.
Inspect input and downstream links where they are recorded. Some artifacts, such as resource logs, may be located outside the project folder.
Use Current, Stale and Missing to choose which artifact states are visible. For example, hide Current to focus on missing outputs.
If no boxes are visible, check the display filters and overall artifact counts. Restore the states you want to inspect.
Click Copy Graphviz to copy the full diagram as DOT text, including nodes hidden by display filters. Paste it into a Graphviz tool to render or save it.
Restore the desired filters and select an artifact again to inspect its details. Use its recorded path and upstream workflow to decide what needs attention.
Click Redraw after project changes to reread the registry. Open Run History for saved settings and logs, or Data Manager for cleanup and archiving.

lessons.title: Prediction Profiler: explore a fitted model
lessons.description: Load model coefficients, vary one input while holding others fixed, and inspect predicted responses.
objectives: Load coefficients with the correct model link.
Sweep one input and adjust held values.
Inspect response curves and sensitivity.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the synthetic coefficient example, or use coefficients from a suitable fitted model. Match its link and input encoding. The coefficient-file route assumes input ranges of zero to one; separate marginal effects are not substitutes for a jointly fitted prediction model.

scenes.narration: Open Regression, then Prediction Profiler to explore predicted responses from a fitted model. The linked example uses synthetic data.
Download and unzip the example, then Browse to the synthetic OLS coefficients CSV. Include the intercept when supplying your own fitted coefficients.
Set Link to the function used by the fitted model. Keep identity for this ordinary least-squares example.
Check the range information after loading. The coefficient-file route assumes each input spans zero to one. Confirm that this matches your intended use before interpreting the curves.
Select Input A for the sweep. Move the held Input B slider to one and inspect the resulting response curve.
Move B to zero and compare the response values. Watch the axis scale as well as the line, because the plot may rescale.
Click Reset held values to return the sliders to the midpoints of their assumed ranges, one half in this example.
Select Input B in the ranked list to sweep B while holding A fixed. The ranking summarizes model sensitivity over its configured input ranges.
Change Points to choose the number of positions evaluated along the plotted curve. Eleven gives a coarser grid than sixty-one without changing the fitted model.
Adjust the held values to explore further scenarios, then reset when finished. Interpret the curves as model predictions and assess real experimental effects with appropriate data.

lessons.title: QC: inspect project quality reports
lessons.description: Choose a project, read available quality reports, investigate warnings and refresh the dashboard.
objectives: Choose the intended project or run.
Read available, missing and outdated reports.
Investigate findings and refresh the view.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a project with saved quality reports. The downloaded Mask and Annotate examples provide different report sets; choose the specific project or run folder you intend to inspect.

scenes.narration: Open QC from Home’s Data category to review quality reports saved with a project.
The header opens Layer Viewer, Control Charts and Outliers. Use their tutorials when a dashboard finding needs further investigation.
Click Browse and choose the project folder. Select the folder containing the reports for the run you want to assess.
Read Missing as an unavailable report for that check. Follow the guidance to obtain the required report before drawing a conclusion.
Choose a run subfolder when its outputs are separate from the parent project. Check that the displayed scope matches the data you intend to review.
Read segmentation warnings and inspect the corresponding fields. For a size-distribution warning, compare the images and object boundaries to understand the cause.
Review the units card alongside the remaining categories. A consistent units report addresses that check; missing reports still need attention.
Read all five categories and their guidance. For leakage, check that sample identities and grouping reflect the intended independent validation units.
Open the details of failures or warnings to identify affected fields and source reports. Use the relevant analysis tool to investigate them.
Click Refresh after reports change on disk. The dashboard rereads available evidence; generate updated reports through the analysis that produces them.
Investigate an out-of-date report against its input data and settings. Keep unresolved findings visible in your project review.
Keep quality reports with the project. Continue in the linked specialist tools or the relevant module tutorial to address each finding.

lessons.title: Image Scatter: inspect measurements and their crops
lessons.description: Plot two measurement columns, preview object crops, and send a selected object to Annotate.
objectives: Load measurements and choose axes.
Inspect the crop behind a point.
Send a selected object to Annotate.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a spaCR measurements database with matching object crops and crop-format files. The downloadable Annotate example provides these inputs.

scenes.narration: Open Image UMAP, then Image Scatter to plot two existing measurements. Use the Annotate example database and its matching cell crops for practice.
Click Browse and open measurements.db. Keep the project’s data folder and crop-format files with the database so thumbnails can be found.
Select cell in the table selector and click Plot. When switching to another table, click Plot again to load its rows.
Set x to cell area and y to cell channel one mean intensity. Axis choices redraw the loaded rows immediately.
Hover over a point to inspect its saved crop and full object identity. Use the image to understand the measurement behind the point.
Move the pointer away to clear the temporary preview, then hover over another point to inspect it.
Swap the x and y measurements to explore the relationship from another view. Choose meaningful features and check their units.
Select another measurement, such as the homogeneity feature. Rows with missing coordinates are omitted from the plot, so the plotted count can differ from the loaded table count.
A constant column, such as measurement dimension in this example, puts the points on a line. Return to a feature with useful variation for object inspection.
To inspect a selected crop in Annotate, first open Annotate and load the same project. Then return to the existing Image Scatter view.
Click the point itself to send its object identity to Annotate, then switch to that page. Hovering only previews the crop.
Inspect the selected object in Annotate before assigning a label. Use Database Browser for table exports, or PCA for component analysis.

lessons.title: Lineage: browse parent objects and their contents
lessons.description: Open stored parent-child relationships, select a family and inspect a matching parent-cell crop in Annotate.
objectives: Load measurements and expand parent-child relationships.
Select objects while checking field and object type.
Open a matching parent-cell crop and obtain the full hierarchy through Python.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the complete Annotate example with its measurements database and matching cell crops. The Graph Builder database-only archive cannot supply images. This example provides cell crops only: use a parent-cell double-click to inspect a crop. The current Open crops family action can substitute unrelated cell crops for missing child crops; avoid that action with this example.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Database Browser, then Lineage. Use the tree to browse which measured objects are stored inside each parent cell.
Browse to measurements.db from the Annotate example and click Build tree. Widen the Object column and divider to read the labels. Identify an object by its field and type as well as its number.
This database contains two thousand three hundred forty-one cells. The tree displays up to two thousand parent families. Use the Python export later in this lesson when you need every family.
Read the summary above the tree. A nucleus counts as a child, so a cell with contents can still have no pathogen object. Use the child types to interpret each family.
Expand a parent to see its children. Here cell three contains nucleus five and pathogen one. Choose the specific object type you want to inspect.
Use Select with contents to select the parent and its children together. The selected identities include their field and object type. Select a child alone when you only need that object.
Expand a large family to inspect its contents. This example includes one family with thirty-three objects. Review the corresponding images when a count looks unusual.
Click a column header to sort the displayed families. Sorting keeps the stored relationships and the two-thousand-parent display limit.
To view crops, first open Annotate and load the matching example project. If you see the message asking for Annotate, open it before requesting images from Lineage.
Use the complete downloaded project, which includes the cell crops. Keep the database and images from the same run together so their object identities match.
Avoid Open crops on a whole family in this example. Missing nucleus and pathogen crops can be replaced by unrelated cell crops. Return to the tree and choose the parent cell alone instead.
Double-click the parent cell in Lineage. Annotate opens that parent’s matching cell crop. This is the crop available in the downloaded example.
Shift-click the parent thumbnail to enlarge its preview, then press Escape to return. An ordinary left click assigns an annotation class, so use Shift when you only want to inspect.

Click Build tree to refresh the view. For the full hierarchy in Python, use read_object_tables, build_forest and lineage_frame, then save the frame as CSV. The linked example CSV contains all seven thousand two hundred one nodes.

lessons.title: Layer Viewer: inspect images and label overlays
lessons.description: Load a matching image and mask, adjust the overlay, and zoom in to inspect object boundaries.
objectives: Open an image and its matching mask.
Adjust visibility, opacity, blending and layer order.
Inspect labels with zoom and pan.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and extract Layer_Viewer_real_image_mask.zip. Use the included intensity image and matching integer-label mask. Physical pixel calibration is unavailable for this example.

scenes.narration: From Home, open QC, then Layer Viewer. Download and extract the linked image-and-mask example. The viewer has its own file controls for these two inputs.
Click plus Image and open fov01_C1 dot tif. The grayscale image appears in the canvas with a percentile contrast stretch for display.
Click Fit to fill the image pane. Fit can stretch a square image in a wide pane; adjust the divider to make the pane approximately square when inspecting shape.
Click plus Mask and open fov01_cell_mask dot tif. The forty-four labelled objects appear over the image. Zero is background and remains transparent.
Select mask in the layer list before changing its controls. Toggle its checkbox to compare the boundaries with the image underneath.
Move mask Opacity to zero to hide its colours while keeping the layer loaded. Check the selected row before adjusting another layer.
Move Opacity to one hundred percent to inspect the label shapes. The colours cover the image inside each labelled object.
Return Opacity to fifty percent and choose translucent blending to see the image texture through the mask. Compare object boundaries with the underlying signal.
Choose additive blending to add the mask colours to the image. Bright areas can saturate in this display, so return to translucent when you need a clearer comparison.
Try multiply and minimum blending to compare darker overlays. These options change the displayed composite while the original intensity values remain available in the source image.

Choose opaque and adjust the Opacity slider to compare its appearance. With this integer mask, fifty-percent opaque blending looks like fifty-percent translucent blending. Restore translucent to continue.
Select image and choose cyan in the colour-map selector. The intensity image changes colour while the mask keeps its label colours. Choose gray to restore the grayscale view.
Select mask and press the down arrow to move it behind the image. The upper layer appears in front. Move the mask up again to inspect its labels.
Click a visible labelled object to read its position and label number in the status line. Use your project metadata when you need to identify that object’s field, plate or well.
Roll the mouse wheel over an object to zoom around the pointer. Move closer until its boundary is easy to inspect.
Hold Shift and drag with the left mouse button to pan. You can also drag with the middle button. Move across the field while keeping the current zoom.
Click Fit to return to the whole field. Adjust the pane shape if the fitted image looks stretched.
Plus Points and plus Shapes add empty auxiliary layers. For drawing or editing segmentation masks, continue in Make Masks; this viewer has no drawing controls for those empty layers.
Select a layer and use Remove to take it out of the view. Its original file remains on disk, ready to load again.

The result is an inspected layer view. For an exported composite, use stack_from_paths and LayerStack.render_uint8 from Python. Continue to Make Masks for saved mask edits or Measure for object measurements.

lessons.title: Graph Builder: plot measurements and filter objects
lessons.description: Load a measurement table, assign plot axes, compare groups and filter the displayed objects.
objectives: Load an example measurement table.
Build a histogram, scatter plot and grouped panels.
Filter objects and choose a follow-up view.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and extract Graph_Builder_real_measurements.zip. It contains measurements.db. To inspect image crops later, also keep the matching Annotate project and its images available.

scenes.narration: Open Graph Builder from Home to explore a measurement table. Start with the linked example database, then repeat the steps with your own measured project.
Click Load table and open measurements dot db from the extracted archive. Choose the cell table. This example contains two thousand three hundred forty-one measured cells.
Find cell_area in the column list and drag it onto X. The automatic chart becomes a histogram: each bar counts cells in an area interval. Check the measurement units before interpreting the axis.
Drag cell_channel_1_mean_intensity onto Y to make a scatter plot. Each point places one cell by its area and channel-one mean intensity. Read the row-count notice when working with larger tables.
Drag columnID onto Colour to distinguish plate columns. Use the legend to match colours to the recorded column labels and look for groups that need closer inspection.

Drag rowID onto the downward facet channel to create a panel for each plate row. Compare the panels using their shared axes. Use independent wells when making statistical comparisons between conditions.

In the filter panel on the right, add cell_area and enter a minimum. The example uses twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five, leaving one thousand one hundred seventy-one rows. Choose thresholds appropriate to your own measurements and watch the plotted count and axes change.
Click Clear all in the filter panel to restore the full table. Use Clear all channels on the left when you want to remove the plot mappings and start a different chart.

Remove a facet with its small cross to return to one scatter plot. Drag a rectangle around objects to select a region. If Open selection in Annotate is unavailable, open Annotate separately with the matching project and inspect objects there.
Click an empty part of the plot to clear the selection. Check the active filters and displayed count before exploring another group of objects.
Use the header shortcuts to open Plate Viewer for well heatmaps or Small Multiples for repeated charts. Keep the source database and your chosen columns and filters so you can reproduce the view.
The current screen displays plots without a chart-export button. Use the Graph Builder API for scripted plots, or Database Browser to export a table for another plotting tool.

lessons.title: AnnData Export: save measured objects and features
lessons.description: Export joined measurements or one object table to h5ad, choose how to handle missing values and retain object metadata.
objectives: Open AnnData Export and select a measured project.
Choose joined or single-table measurements and a missing-value policy.
Export an h5ad file with feature names and object metadata.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a project that has completed Measure, or download the measurements example through Annotate. Work on a copy of the project and retain its source images. Use the current nightly build for the normal exporter shown here.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Measure, then choose AnnData Export. Use this tool to save measured objects, their features and their metadata together in an h5ad file.
Select your measured project as Source. For this walkthrough, use a copy of the measurements example available through Annotate. Keep its measurements folder and source images together.
Leave Single table empty to combine the selected tables onto cell rows. Set an output filename ending in h5ad. Keep float32 and gzip for a compact numerical export.
Set Row limit to zero to include every available row. A positive limit is useful for a small first export. Leave Compute UMAP off when you only need the measurement matrix.

Choose keep as the missing-value policy, then press Run. Read the completion message. The joined example contains two thousand three hundred forty-one cell rows and one thousand one hundred thirty-six features.
Set Single table to cell and choose a new output filename. Run again to export the cell measurements alone. Here, the result has two hundred sixty-one features and twenty-eight missing values.

Choose mean to replace missing feature values with observed column means. The export also records their original positions in a missing-value layer. Use this policy when mean imputation fits your downstream analysis.
Choose drop_features to remove columns containing missing values. This example retains all cells and removes four feature columns. Check the retained feature names when comparing exports.
Choose drop_objects to remove rows containing missing feature values. Seven cells are removed here. Consider whether the excluded objects could change your analysis.
Choose nucleus as the single table when you need one row per nucleus. This example produces two thousand six hundred eighty-two nuclei and three hundred forty-one features.

Enable Register artifact to make the output discoverable in the project. Save each policy under a distinct filename and retain its settings. The h5ad file contains measurements and metadata; keep the source images separately.

Open the resulting h5ad file in your downstream analysis and inspect its shape, feature names and object metadata. From Python, run_anndata_export uses the same settings, while build_anndata constructs the data in memory.

lessons.title: PCA: explore measurements and export components
lessons.description: Load measured objects, choose features, compare principal components and export scores, loadings and explained variance.
objectives: Load a measurement database or CSV and select features.
Choose scaling, missing-value handling and filters.
Inspect component scores and loadings, then export three result tables.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the example from the Annotate tutorial and work with a copy of measurements.db. This walkthrough uses its cell table, with 2,341 measured objects across four wells. Keep the original database and record your feature list, filters, scaling and missing-value policy.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Image UMAP, then choose PCA. Use PCA to summarize several measurement columns as principal components. Start with the measurements database from the linked Annotate example.
Click Load table beside the PCA heading. Open measurements.db and select cell. Check the displayed table and object count. You can also load a CSV containing measurement columns.

Clear the feature search and click None to untick all visible features. Select cell_area, cell_channel_1_mean_intensity and cell_perimeter. Clear the search again, set Components to three, then click Run PCA.

Keep Scale on Standardise to center each feature and divide by its sample standard deviation. Read the scree plot: the first two components explain about sixty-five point seven and thirty-one point seven percent of the selected features’ variance.
Choose rowID in Colour, PC three on X and PC one on Y. These controls redraw the fitted result. Each point represents a cell; rowID identifies a spatial row in this example.

Return to PC one and PC two. Toggle Loadings biplot to show or hide feature arrows. The arrows show correlations with the displayed components; use their directions and the dashed reference circle to compare features.

Choose Centre only to fit using the original measurement scales. The first component now explains about ninety point one percent. Scaling changes the question being summarized. Restore Standardise to compare features on a common scale.

In the right-hand filter, add cell_area and set the minimum to twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The panel refits PCA on the remaining one thousand one hundred seventy-one cells, so both the population and component directions change.

Click Clear all in the filter to restore the full population. Check the object count after filtering. The source database stays unchanged; the displayed result is recalculated for the chosen population.

Select cell_channel_0_homogeneity_distance_32 as a fourth feature. Click Run PCA to include it in the result. This example has seven missing measurements in that column; use NaN to choose how the fit handles them.

With Auto, features missing in more than two percent of rows are removed, then incomplete rows are dropped. Here all four features remain and seven cells are excluded. Read the report to see the features and objects actually analyzed.

Choose Drop features to remove any selected feature containing missing values. In this example the texture feature is removed and all cells remain. The result notice shows which features were excluded, even while their checkboxes remain ticked.

Choose Mean-impute to retain all cells and features by replacing missing values with the observed feature mean during calculation. Here seven values are replaced. Record this choice when presenting the result; the replacements are estimates.

Choose Complete cases to retain the selected features and exclude incomplete rows. To return to the original example, choose Auto, untick the texture feature, clear the search, click Run PCA and set Colour to none.

Click Export and choose a base name such as pca_example. The panel writes three CSV files: scores for analyzed objects, loadings and correlations for features, and explained variance for components. The scores table also includes the source measurement columns.

Open the exported tables and keep them with your feature list, filters and analysis settings. Treat the cells as observations within their wells when interpreting separation. For a repeatable Python analysis, use pca and PCASpec from spacr.qt.widgets.pca_model.

lessons.title: Tabulate: summarize measurements by well and field
lessons.description: Group measured objects, select summary statistics, inspect missing groups and export a pivot table or send it to Graph Builder.
objectives: Load measurements and group them by well or field.
Choose values, statistics and filters while checking contributing counts.
Export CSV summaries and refresh their Graph Builder plots.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the measurement example from the Annotate tutorial and work with a copy of measurements.db. Its cell table has 2,341 objects across four wells. Keep spatial labels distinct from treatment labels, and choose the grouping level appropriate to your experiment.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Database Browser, then choose Tabulate. Use this tool to summarize measurement columns by well, field or another group. This walkthrough uses the database from the linked Annotate example.

Inside Tabulate, click Load table, open measurements.db and choose cell. Use Tabulate’s own controls to select its input and export. Check the table and the two thousand three hundred forty-one loaded objects.

Choose Plate slash row slash column to group by plate and well. Leave Values empty to count source rows. The four wells contain six hundred fifteen, five hundred twenty-five, seven hundred and five hundred one cells.

Search for fieldID and drag it into Columns. This creates a well-by-field grid. Hover over a blank cell to inspect it: this example has one combination with no source rows. Keep that distinct from a measured zero.

Clear Columns, then drag cell_area into Values. The default summary shows count, mean and sample standard deviation. Searching finds column names; changing the axes or statistics recomputes the summary.
Hover over a result cell to see all its statistics and the contributing count, including lines hidden by the row height. Standard deviation describes variation among the objects in that group.

Enable median, sem and quantile to add those statistics. Set Quantile at to zero point seven five for the upper quartile. SEM uses the available object count; choose the experimental replicate level separately when estimating biological uncertainty.

Set Quantile at to zero point five to display the median. The first well now shows twenty-two thousand four hundred for both. Restore zero point seven five and switch off the extra statistics to return to the simpler summary.

Replace cell_area with cell_channel_0_homogeneity_distance_32. This feature has seven missing values, so its contributing counts are smaller than the source-row counts. Use those counts when comparing groups.

Restore cell_area and click Export CSV inside Tabulate. Choose a new filename. This well summary contains the three grouping keys, count, mean and standard deviation. Keep your grouping, statistic and filter choices beside the exported file.

Click Plot this table to send the summary to Graph Builder. Drag columnID onto X, mean onto Y and rowID onto Colour. Check the inferred column types: Automatic treats these four distinct means as categories in this example and displays a heatmap.

Add a cell_area filter with a minimum of twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The pivot updates immediately for the remaining objects. Click Plot this table again whenever you want to transfer the updated summary to the chart.

After clicking Plot this table, inspect the updated group means. An area-filter note can appear because the transferred summary contains mean rather than cell_area. The object filter has already been applied upstream in Tabulate.
Click Clear all in the filter, then Plot this table again to restore the original well summary. Save filtered and unfiltered exports under different names when you need both.

For a field-level summary, drag fieldID into Rows after the well keys. Each populated row now summarizes one field within a well. Inspect the contributing counts and keep this grouping level consistent when comparing results.

Click Plot this table, put fieldID on X, keep mean on Y and rowID on Colour, then choose Scatter from Plot. In this example mean is now recognized as continuous. Confirm the displayed column types and axis labels.

The scatter plot displays fifty-one field means. Colours identify spatial rows, and repeated field labels can belong to different wells. Use the original object table when you want to select individual cells and inspect their images.

Export the field summary as a separate CSV. It contains fifty-two grid rows, with the empty combination left blank; the chart contains fifty-one populated groups. For Python, use pivot and PivotSpec from spacr.qt.widgets.pivot_spec, then to_csv to save the result.

lessons.title: Feature Dictionary: find definitions and units
lessons.description: Search by measurement name or concept, read the definition and units, and copy useful reference text.
objectives: Find a definition by name or concept.
Narrow the results with concept and object filters.
Read units and notes, then copy the definition.
lessons.prerequisite: Have a measurement column name ready, or start with an idea such as size or intensity. The built-in dictionary can be opened without loading a project.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Feature Dictionary. Use this window when you want to understand a measurement column in a results table or plot.
Type size in the search field and select Area from the results. The definition appears on the right, and the matching list updates as you type.
Choose a concept and object type to narrow the definitions. Try intensity and cell. Reset the selectors to Any concept and Any object for a broader search.
Search for cell_channel_1_mean_intensity and select Mean intensity. Read the statistic and units to understand what the column describes.
Scroll down to Channel, Module and Computed by for more detail. Use the named computing function as a starting point in the API reference.

Look up cell_area and read Unit. In two-dimensional measurements it represents area; in three-dimensional measurements it represents volume. Check the measurement units recorded in your project before converting values.

Read Note for qualifications such as values already expressed in physical units. For a dictionary of the columns actually present in a database, use describe_database and export_dictionary from Python.
If no definitions match, clear the filters and try a broader term or the exact column name. Custom features may need documentation from the workflow that created them.
Select the definition text and copy it into your notes. Use the Python export functions when you need a project-specific dictionary file, then return to your table or plot.

lessons.title: Small Multiples: compare groups with shared or separate axes
lessons.description: Load measurements, arrange grouped scatter plots, choose axis scales and filters, and add a derived column.
objectives: Load measurements and assign axes and facets.
Choose shared, independent or grouped axis limits.
Inspect filters and displayed groups, then add or remove a derived column.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the measurement example from the Annotate tutorial and work with a copy of measurements.db. This walkthrough uses its cell table, with 2,341 objects across four wells. Small Multiples displays plots; use Tabulate to export grouped CSV summaries.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Graph Builder, then Small Multiples. Use this view to compare the same measurements across groups. This example uses the measurements database available from the linked Annotate tutorial.

Click Load table beside the Small Multiples heading. Open a copy of measurements.db and select cell. Check the table and its two thousand three hundred forty-one objects before assigning plot channels.

Drag cell_area onto X and cell_channel_1_mean_intensity onto Y, then choose Scatter. Put rowID on Facet down and columnID on Facet across. Search helps you find column names; each point represents a measured cell.
Choose shared for both scales so all four panels use matching axis limits. Read the group titles and object counts. In this example the facet labels identify spatial rows and columns.
Choose free for X scale and Y scale to give each panel its own limits. This makes within-group patterns easier to see. Compare tick labels carefully because the ranges now differ between panels.
Choose per row for both scales to share limits between panels on each grid row. Different rows can have different ranges. Use this when comparisons within rows are the priority.
Choose per column to share limits within each grid column. You can set X and Y independently. Restore shared on both axes when you want to compare all four wells on common scales.

In Filter, add cell_area and set its minimum to twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The grid updates immediately for the remaining one thousand one hundred seventy-one objects. Check the new panel counts.

Click Clear all in Filter to restore the full population. Use Clear all channels on the left when you want to remove the chart assignments instead. Both operations leave the source database unchanged.

Filter columnID to c two and fieldID to f twenty and f twenty-one. Put fieldID on Facet across and keep rowID on Facet down. The row-five, field-twenty panel has no objects; its empty panel represents a missing group.
Clear the filters and restore columnID on Facet across. Set Wrap at to five. Wrapping applies to a single facet channel, so the current two-way grid stays two by two.
Clear Facet down and put fieldID on Facet across. With Wrap at five, the displayed fields fill rows of up to five panels. Unused slots at the end are hidden.

Read the notice below the grid before comparing groups. This view displays twelve field levels; field twenty-one is omitted from the panels. The loaded-row count includes that field, so check which groups are actually visible.

Turn wrapping off and restore rowID and columnID as the two facets. In Columns, name a derived column area_k and enter cell_area divided by one thousand. Check the preview, then click Add column to compute it for the full table.

Drag area_k onto X to display area in thousands of the original units. The vertical coordinates and groups stay the same. This rescales numbers; physical-area conversion requires the correct image calibration.
Put cell_area back on X. Select area_k in Columns and click Remove to delete the derived column from this view. Keep a record of your variables, facets, filters and scale choices.

Use Tabulate when you need an exported CSV summary. For scripted small-multiple plots, use trellis and TrellisSpec from spacr.qt.widgets.trellis_spec with GraphSpec for the chart channels. Interpret the groups at the appropriate experimental replicate level.

lessons.title: Gate Editor: select populations and save their membership
lessons.description: Draw gates on measurements, save reusable boundaries, explore projections and export object membership to a database.
objectives: Load measurements and draw named gates.
Save and reload gate strategies, figures and membership.
Explore three-dimensional views, clustering and filters.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the Annotate example and make a working copy of measurements.db. Gate Editor uses its 2,341 cell measurements; it has no separate example-download button. Export gates writes membership to the chosen database. Gate names should describe the selected measurements until their biological meaning has been established.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Tools and choose Gate Editor. Adjust the dividers so you can see the plot, gate table and side controls. Use the measurement database from the Annotate example.

Click Load table, open your working copy of measurements.db and choose cell. The example contains two thousand three hundred forty-one objects. Keep a copy because Export gates writes membership to this database.
Choose cell_area for X and cell_channel_1_mean_intensity for Y, then select Rectangle. Each point represents an object. Check the feature names and units before drawing.
Drag across the scatter, release and enter a descriptive gate name. The gate stores boundaries in the two selected measurements.

Read the count and percentage beside the gate name. The illustrated region contains six hundred fifty-five objects. Your mouse positions may give different boundaries; save a strategy to repeat an exact selection.
Untick the gate to hide its overlay, then tick it to show it again. Delete gate removes its definition. The Filter tab separately controls the objects displayed beneath the gates.
Click Save gates to write a JSON strategy. Delete the gate, then choose Load gates and open the saved file. Reuse strategies with matching feature names, units and preprocessing.
The loaded strategy restores the saved boundaries and population. Check the axes, outline and count before continuing with another dataset.
Choose Save graph to save the plotted figure. File formats follow your plotting preferences; this example produces PNG and PDF. Keep the JSON strategy beside the figure.
Choose Export gates to write membership flags to the working database’s filters table. Each flag is associated with the object’s plate, well, field, label and type.
Draw a second gate and give it a new name. New shapes are independent of the selected gate, so the second can include objects outside the first. Save this two-gate strategy under a new filename.
Choose three D and set Z to cell_perimeter. Use the spin-axis buttons to rotate the view. Return to two D to inspect the original area-intensity boundaries.
Use From view to create a named box bounded by the three displayed measurements. Check its population count and save the new strategy separately.
Enable x D to compute principal components from eligible measurements. The axis labels show explained variance for each component. Choose two D or three D separately to control the view.

When turning x D off, select the raw measurement axes again. Save projection details separately: the gate JSON does not retain the fitted projection, and component boundaries may differ between independently fitted datasets.

Open Search and widen its panel. Save and remove temporary gates, choose the two raw features, enable scaling and set twenty minimum neighbours and five Walk steps. Click Run walk and review the confirmation values.
Inspect the resulting outlines and population counts. Here Walk chooses a radius near zero point one six seven and finds two populations. Review which objects lie outside those regions.
Save the Walk strategy, remove its gates and switch Walk off. Try radius zero point five to compare the resulting larger region, then choose the strategy appropriate to your analysis.
Reload the saved two-gate strategy. In Filter, add cell_area with a minimum of twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The view now contains one thousand one hundred seventy-one objects.
Click Clear all to restore the full population. Check the active filters and gate definitions before interpreting counts or exporting membership.
To inspect the loaded table directly, open the right-hand console and enter len(df). This example returns two thousand three hundred forty-one rows.
Keep your data, JSON strategy and exported membership together. In Python, use GateSet for definitions, gate_mask_over_table to calculate membership and export_gate to save object flags.

lessons.title: Feature Explorer: compare groups and export a feature ranking
lessons.description: Choose a grouping column, rank measurements by AUC or KS, inspect distributions and export the selected features.
objectives: Load measurements and choose the comparison groups.
Read rankings and distributions, then explore filters and computed columns.
Export the intended number of ranked features.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the Annotate example and open a working copy of its measurements.db. It contains 2,341 cells. This walkthrough compares rowID groups r12 and r5, which identify spatial plate rows. Choose a group column appropriate to your own experiment and account for cells sharing wells when interpreting the comparison.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify, then Feature Explorer. Use the measurement database from the Annotate example to compare existing features between groups.
Click Load table, choose measurements.db and select cell. Set Split by to rowID. The example groups are spatial plate rows; check that your grouping column represents the comparison you intend.
Choose AUC under Rank by. Separation is the absolute value of twice AUC minus one. Higher in shows the direction, and min n counts finite measurements in the smaller group.
Set Top to four to inspect four overlaid histograms. Within each feature the groups share bin edges, and bar heights show counts. Read both the distributions and the ranking score.
Click Export ranking to save the displayed top features. With Top set to four, the export contains four feature rows. Increase Top before exporting a longer ranking.
Set Top to five hundred to include all two hundred sixty-one scorable features in this example. The plot shows at most eight distributions, even when the exported ranking is longer.
Switch Rank by to KS to compare the largest gap between cumulative distributions. KS can reveal spread differences missed by AUC. Return to AUC to inspect direction through Higher in.
In Filter, add cell_area and set the minimum to twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The population changes to one thousand one hundred seventy-one cells, and the ranking updates.
Click Clear all to restore the full population and ranking. Recheck Split by after changing filters so you know which groups are being compared.
Filtering rowID to r12 removes the second group. In this build, Split by then changes automatically to another column. Check that control whenever a filter removes a group.

Clear the filter and explicitly restore rowID under Split by. Keep Shuffle test off for this example: cells share wells, so unrestricted cell-label shuffles do not represent independent experimental replicates.

Open Columns and name a computed column area_k. Enter cell_area divided by one thousand and click Add column with replacement off. Preview displays the first two thousand rows; adding applies the formula to the whole table.
The computed column joins the ranking. Positive rescaling gives it the same AUC and KS as cell_area. Remove the formula to return to the original features.

Export the ranking after checking the population, Split by and Top. For Python, use rank_features and ExplorerSpec from spacr.qt.widgets.feature_rank. Continue with Graph Builder to plot a selected feature in more detail.

lessons.title: Outliers: flag measurements for inspection
lessons.description: Choose features and a robust rule, inspect object and well results, and export flags with the full input table.
objectives: Load measurements and select the features to scan.
Compare MAD, IQR and log-transformed rules.
Read scoring limitations and export rows, flags and a report.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a working copy of measurements.db from the Annotate example. Flags identify observations for inspection; choose thresholds for your analysis.
